title: John
subtitle: All Twenty-One Chapters - Key Notes, Cross-References, and Prophecy Fulfilled (WEB)

items.value: This book walks through all twenty-one chapters of John, one chapter at a time, with the full text of every chapter printed in it. It grew out of study guides written for a group working through the Gospels three chapters at a time, and it is the sixth volume in this series.

John is the Gospel that starts before the beginning. Matthew opens with a family tree, Mark with a man in the desert, Luke with a historian describing his method. John opens with the first words of Genesis and carries them back past the first day: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Then, fourteen verses later, the sentence the whole book rests on: the Word became flesh, and pitched His tent among us.
It is a companion to the Jeremiah, Matthew, Malachi, Mark and Luke volumes in this series, and it is built the same way. If you have used any of those, everything here will be familiar.

The prose is the point. The tables and footnotes are apparatus - useful, and worth using - but they exist to serve a reading of John, not to replace one. If you only ever read the chapter introductions and the scripture text, you will have read this book properly.

sections.heading: How this book is put together

items.value: Every chapter follows the same shape.

values: **Key Notes** - the observations worth having in hand before you read: a word that carries more than the translation shows, a custom the first readers took for granted, a connection to something earlier in the book. Each note ends with the verses it comes from.
**Key Cross-References** - passages that stand behind or alongside the chapter, grouped by theme.
**Prophecy Fulfilled** - places where the chapter runs back into the Hebrew Scriptures. The heading is shared with the Matthew, Mark and Luke volumes, and there is a note about it below.
**For Further Study** - three places to go deeper.
**Introduction** - the chapter read as a whole before you read it in parts.
**The chapter itself**, printed in full in the World English Bible, with footnote markers on the verses the references belong to.

items.value: Every scripture reference in the book is a live link to the World English Bible on BibleGateway. In the app, tapping a footnote marker shows the full text of the passages cited and a line on why they connect, so you can follow a cross-reference without losing your place.

sections.heading: A note on the second table

items.value: The second table in each chapter is headed **Prophecy Fulfilled**, the same as in the other three Gospels, so that anyone reading across them is not relearning the apparatus halfway through.

John uses the fulfillment formula less than Matthew, and saves most of it for the last week - the betrayal, the garments divided, the bones not broken, the side pierced. His more usual way is to show Yahshua standing where something earlier stood: the tabernacle, the manna, the bronze serpent lifted up, the shepherd, the vine, the Passover lamb. That is typology, a pattern answered by a Person, and many of the entries in the table are of that kind. Where an entry is a pattern rather than a prediction, the note at the verse says so.

sections.heading: A note on the divine names

items.value: In the notes and introductions this book uses **Yahweh** for the covenant name of God and **Yahshua** for the Messiah, as the group this material was written for does.

The printed scripture text is never altered. The World English Bible reads Jesus in the Gospels, and it stands exactly as the translators set it. So you will see Yahshua in a paragraph of commentary and Jesus in the verse beneath it. That is deliberate. It keeps our own speech and the translator's work visibly distinct.

sections.heading: A note on the chapter titles

items.value: The chapter titles in this book are not traditional and are not found in any Bible. They were written for this study - they name what struck us in that chapter rather than summarising it.

sections.heading: A note on the disputed passages

items.value: Two passages in John are missing from the earliest manuscripts. This book prints both, as the World English Bible does, and says plainly where the question lies.

**John 5:3-4** - the angel who stirred the water of the pool, and the first one in being healed. Absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts. Whether John wrote it or a copyist explained the scene, the sick man's own words in verse 7 show that this is what the people lying there believed.

**John 7:53-8:11** - the woman taken in adultery. Missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts of John and found in different places in later ones. Most readers believe it is a true account of Yahshua that was preserved separately and later placed here. Its language and setting fit His last week in Jerusalem.
This book prints them because the WEB prints them, notes the evidence at the verse, and leaves the judgment where it belongs.

The book never names its author. It points to him instead: "the disciple whom Jesus loved," who leans against Him at the last supper, stands at the cross, outruns Peter to the tomb, and recognises the Lord on the shore. The last chapter says plainly that this is the disciple who wrote these things, and that others know his testimony is true.

The earliest tradition identifies him as John the son of Zebedee, one of the twelve, writing late in life. The Gospel never uses John's own name for him - the only John in this book is the Baptist - which is hard to explain unless the author was deliberately keeping himself out of it.

What the book does show is a man who knew Jerusalem before it fell: the pool with five porches, the pavement called Gabbatha, the brook Kidron, Solomon's porch in winter, the hour of the day a thing happened, and how many fish were in a net.
John tells you, which no other Gospel writer does so directly. "These are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name."

Every story in the book was chosen for that purpose. He says plainly that Yahshua did many other signs, and that the world could not hold the books if all of them were written. What is here is a selection, made on purpose, aimed at belief.

values: **The Prologue** (1:1-18) - the Word before the beginning, and the Word made flesh.
**The Signs** (1:19-12:50) - a public ministry marked by seven signs and by the feasts of Israel, ending with Isaiah's question: who has believed our report?
**The Glory** (13:1-20:31) - one night of teaching in private, then the cross, which John calls glory, and the resurrection.
**The Epilogue** (21:1-25) - breakfast on the beach and Peter restored.

items.value: The seven signs usually counted are the water made wine, the official's son healed, the man at the pool, the five thousand fed, the walk on the water, the man born blind, and Lazarus raised. John numbers only the first two and lets the reader keep count.

Seven times Yahshua says I am with a picture attached: the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way and the truth and the life, and the true vine.

Alongside those are the times He says I am with nothing after it at all - to the woman at the well, on the water at night, before Abraham was, and in the garden, when an armed company falls to the ground. In Greek it is ego eimi, the phrase the Greek Scriptures use for Yahweh's own words in Isaiah: that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. John wants you to hear it.

No Gospel pays more attention to the appointed times. John marks three Passovers, which is where the familiar reckoning of a ministry of about three years comes from. He sets three whole chapters at Tabernacles, where Yahshua offers living water on the last great day and calls Himself the light of the world beside the lamps of the feast. He records Him in the temple at Dedication. And he dates the cross to the Preparation Day of the Passover, with the Lamb of God dying as the lambs were made ready.

John is also the Gospel that dates the last supper "before the feast of the Passover," and has the leaders the next morning still waiting to eat it. The notes at those chapters follow John's own time markers.

sections.heading: How John differs from the other three

items.value: Readers coming from Matthew, Mark and Luke notice the difference at once. There are no parables in the usual sense, and no casting out of demons. Much of the action is in Judea and Jerusalem rather than Galilee. The teaching comes in long conversations - with Nicodemus, with the woman at the well, with the crowds at the feasts, with the disciples on the last night - rather than in short sayings.
Most of what is in John is in no other Gospel. The early church described it as the spiritual Gospel, written by someone who knew the others and set out to tell what they had not.

Tradition places John last of the four, toward the end of the first century, written from Ephesus. Some scholars argue for an earlier date, pointing out that John describes the pool by the sheep gate as standing - there is a pool - in the present tense. This book does not try to settle it.
Read John straight through before any of the apparatus. It can be read in an evening, and the pattern of the signs and the feasts only shows if you see the whole.
After that, take a chapter at a time. Read the introduction first, then the chapter itself, and come back to the notes and tables afterward; they will mean more once the text is in you.
If you are reading with others, the introductions are written to be read aloud. That is what they were for originally, and they still work best that way.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 1 - The Word Made Flesh, a Voice That Claims Nothing, and Come and See
chapters.title: The Word Made Flesh, a Voice That Claims Nothing, and Come and See
keyNotes: "In the beginning" is the first phrase of Genesis, quoted deliberately. John is not starting his book; he is starting the book, and going back further than Genesis does (John 1:1).

Logos was a live word in two worlds at once. To a Greek it was the ordering principle behind everything; to a Jew it was the davar, the word by which God creates and by which prophets are addressed, and the Aramaic paraphrases used it as a way of speaking about God Himself acting. John picks the one word that lands in both rooms (John 1:1).

"The Word was God" lacks the article before God in the Greek, which is sometimes offered as a reason to read a god. But Greek regularly drops the article from a predicate noun standing before its verb, and John writes the same construction elsewhere without anyone reading it that way. The grammar is worth knowing rather than shouting about (John 1:1).
Verse 3 is deliberately airtight: all things were made through him, and without him not one thing was made that has been made. There is no category left over (John 1:3).
The verb in verse 5 can mean overcome or grasp, and both senses are alive in it - the darkness neither put the light out nor understood it. The WEB prints overcome (John 1:5).

The witness is introduced before the incarnation is stated. John the Baptist arrives in verse 6, eight verses before the Word becomes flesh, because in this Gospel testimony always comes first (John 1:6-8).
Verse 11 uses two different forms: he came to his own things - his own place - and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11).
"He gave the right to become God's children" is exousia, authority, and the birth is defined by three negations: not of blood, not of the will of the flesh, not of the will of a man (John 1:12-13).
"Lived among us" is eskenosen - he pitched his tent, he tabernacled. The word is built on the tent in the wilderness, and the next clause, we saw his glory, is what filled it (John 1:14).

"Grace and truth" is the Hebrew pair chesed and emet - loyal love and faithfulness - which is what Yahweh proclaimed over Moses on the mountain. Three verses later Moses is named by name (John 1:14, 17).
Verse 17 is not law bad, grace good. The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came into being through Yahshua. One was handed down and the other arrived in person (John 1:17).
"In the bosom of the Father" is the position of the honoured guest reclining next to the host at a meal. John uses the same phrase later of the disciple leaning on Yahshua (John 1:18, 13:23).
The delegation asks three questions in descending order of expectation: the Christ, Elijah, the prophet of Deuteronomy 18. John says no to all three (John 1:19-21).

He denies being Elijah, and Yahshua later says he came in the spirit and power of Elijah. Both are true at different levels - he is not the returned prophet, and he is doing the work Malachi described. This book flags the tension rather than flattening it (John 1:21, Luke 1:17).
The only identity he claims is a sound. I am a voice. Not a title, not an office - the noise somebody makes ahead of a king (John 1:23).
Loosening a sandal was slave work, and rabbinic tradition held that a Hebrew slave could not be made to do it. He says he is not fit for the job a slave would be spared (John 1:27).

"Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" appears nowhere else in the Gospels. Which lamb is not specified - the Passover lamb, which was not a sin offering; the silent lamb of Isaiah 53; the daily offering in the temple; the ram caught for Isaac. The ambiguity may well be the point (John 1:29).

The opening chapter is dated in days - the next day, the next day, again the next day - and chapter 2 opens on the third day after that. Counted through, it makes a week. Many readers see a creation week deliberately laid over the start of the Gospel; the text does not say so outright (John 1:29, 35, 43, 2:1).
"It was about the tenth hour" is four in the afternoon. Nothing in the story depends on it, which is exactly why it reads like something somebody remembered (John 1:39).
Andrew first finds his own brother. That is the shape of the whole chapter - found, and then brought. Nobody in it is argued into anything (John 1:41-42).
John translates Rabbi, Messiah and Cephas for his reader. He is writing for people who do not have the Aramaic (John 1:38, 41, 42).
Nazareth is never mentioned anywhere in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Nathanael is from Cana, the next village over. His remark is small-town rivalry rather than theology (John 1:46, 21:2).

"An Israelite in whom is no deceit" is a pointed thing to say, because Israel was the name given to a man whose whole early life was deceit - and the promise three verses later is Jacob's dream (John 1:47, 51).
Being under a fig tree is sometimes read as rabbinic shorthand for studying Torah. It may be. The text simply says he was there and that he was seen (John 1:48).

The last verse is Genesis 28 with a Person where the ladder was - heaven opened, and the angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man. And the you is plural: the promise is to all of them (John 1:51).

intro: Every other Gospel begins somewhere a reader can stand. Matthew begins with a family tree, Mark with a man in a desert, Luke with a historian describing his method. John begins before there was anywhere to stand.

In the beginning was the Word is a quotation, and every Jewish reader knew of what. John picks up the first sentence of Genesis and carries it back past the first day. And the term he chooses is live in two worlds at once: to a Greek the Logos is the reason behind the universe, the pattern holding it together; to a Jew the word of Yahweh is how the world was made, and in the Aramaic paraphrases read in synagogue the Word was a way of speaking about God acting without naming Him directly. It is the one term that lands in both rooms - and then John says the thing neither room was ready for. The Word became flesh.

The verb is not lived but pitched a tent: he tabernacled among us. It is built on the tent in the middle of the wilderness camp, the one with the glory over it that Moses could not walk into - and the very next clause is that we beheld his glory. What filled the tent moved into a body. And the pair that goes with it, grace and truth, is chesed and emet, the two words Yahweh speaks over Himself as He passes in front of Moses on the mountain, which is why Moses is named three verses later. That verse is not law bad and grace good. The law was given - handed down, delivered. Grace and truth came into being, arrived in a person. The same God, and the second time He has a face.

Then a man in the wilderness handles an interrogation by refusing every title offered him. Not the Christ, not Elijah, not the prophet. Asked to supply something his questioners can take back, he claims to be a sound - a voice, the noise somebody makes ahead of a king. And when he finally points, the sentence puts the whole book in one line: behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. He never says which lamb, and there were several available - Passover, the silent lamb of Isaiah, the offering made every morning and evening, the ram caught in the thicket when Abraham raised the knife. The refusal to narrow it may be the point.

The rest of the chapter is people finding people. Andrew follows, then fetches his brother. Philip fetches Nathanael, and when Nathanael sneers about Nazareth - which is village rivalry rather than theology, since Cana is the next town over - Philip does not argue with him but says come and see, which is what Yahshua had already said to the first two. There is no debate anywhere in this chapter. And the man greeted as an Israelite without deceit is being handed a loaded compliment, because Israel was the name given to a man whose early life was deceit; the promise made to him a few verses later is that man's dream at Bethel, the ladder with traffic moving between heaven and earth. Except that in this version there is no ladder. There is a Person.

verses.7: The same came as a witness, that he might testify about the light, that all might believe through him.

verses.10: He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world didn’t recognize him.

verses.14: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.
verses.15: John testified about him. He cried out, saying, “This was he of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me has surpassed me, for he was before me.’”
verses.16: From his fullness we all received grace upon grace.
verses.17: For the law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realized through Jesus Christ.
verses.18: No one has seen God at any time. The one and only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.
verses.19: This is John’s testimony, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”
verses.20: He declared, and didn’t deny, but he declared, “I am not the Christ.”
verses.21: They asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the prophet?” He answered, “No.”
verses.22: They said therefore to him, “Who are you? Give us an answer to take back to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”
verses.23: He said, “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said.”
verses.24: The ones who had been sent were from the Pharisees.
verses.25: They asked him, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?”
verses.26: John answered them, “I baptize in water, but among you stands one whom you don’t know.
verses.27: He is the one who comes after me, who is preferred before me, whose sandal strap I’m not worthy to loosen.”
verses.28: These things were done in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
verses.29: The next day, he saw Jesus coming to him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
verses.30: This is he of whom I said, ‘After me comes a man who is preferred before me, for he was before me.’
verses.31: I didn’t know him, but for this reason I came baptizing in water: that he would be revealed to Israel.”
verses.32: John testified, saying, “I have seen the Spirit descending like a dove out of heaven, and it remained on him.
verses.33: I didn’t recognize him, but he who sent me to baptize in water, he said to me, ‘On whomever you will see the Spirit descending, and remaining on him, the same is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’
verses.34: I have seen, and have testified that this is the Son of God.”
verses.35: Again, the next day, John was standing with two of his disciples,
verses.36: and he looked at Jesus as he walked, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!”
verses.37: The two disciples heard him speak, and they followed Jesus.
verses.38: Jesus turned, and saw them following, and said to them, “What are you looking for?” They said to him, “Rabbi” (which is to say, being interpreted, Teacher), “where are you staying?”
verses.39: He said to them, “Come, and see.” They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour.
verses.40: One of the two who heard John, and followed him, was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.
verses.41: He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ).
verses.42: He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him, and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (which is by interpretation, Peter).
verses.43: On the next day, he was determined to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.”
verses.44: Now Philip was from Bethsaida, of the city of Andrew and Peter.
verses.45: Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, “We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”
verses.46: Nathanael said to him, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”
verses.47: Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said about him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!”
verses.48: Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”
verses.49: Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!”
verses.50: Jesus answered him, “Because I told you, ‘I saw you underneath the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these!”
verses.51: He said to him, “Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 2 - Six Stone Jars, a Whip of Cords, and a Temple Raised in Three Days
chapters.title: Six Stone Jars, a Whip of Cords, and a Temple Raised in Three Days
keyNotes: "The third day" counts on from the days marked through chapter 1. Taken together the opening runs to seven, which many readers take as a creation week laid over the beginning of the Gospel (John 2:1, 1:29).
Cana appears only in John, and the one man we know from there is Nathanael, who was called two days earlier (John 2:1, 21:2).
"Woman" sounds cold in English and was not rude in Greek - He uses the same address to her from the cross. But it is not mother either, and the distance in it is real (John 2:4, 19:26).
"What does that have to do with you and me" is a Hebrew idiom that turns up in Samuel and Kings. It means this is not a matter we share, and it is not affectionate (John 2:4).
"My hour has not yet come" is the first of a series. The hour finally arrives when He says the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified - and He means the cross (John 2:4, 12:23).
Whatever he says to you, do it, is the last thing His mother says in the whole of Scripture. She is not recorded speaking again (John 2:5).

The jars are stone rather than clay because stone does not contract ritual impurity - which is why the vessels for purification water were made of it. Two or three metretes apiece puts the total somewhere near a hundred and twenty gallons (John 2:6).
He takes the water kept for ceremonial washing and makes it the wine of a wedding. Nothing is destroyed and nothing is condemned; the same water is put to a better use (John 2:7-9).
There were six jars. Seven is the number that would have been complete (John 2:6).
The master of the feast does not know where it came from; the servants who drew it do. In this Gospel knowledge keeps landing on the people who did what they were told (John 2:9).
The compliment goes to a bridegroom who did nothing. The next chapter will name who the bridegroom actually is (John 2:10, 3:29).
John calls it a sign - semeion - not a mighty work, which is the Synoptics' usual word. A mighty work displays power; a sign points away from itself at something else (John 2:11).

John puts the clearing of the temple at the start of the ministry and the other three put it at the end. Either there were two, three years apart, or John has placed it here for reasons of theme rather than sequence. Both readings have serious defenders and this book does not settle it (John 2:13-16).

The whip is only in John, and read closely it is used on the animals. To the men selling doves He speaks instead - and doves were the offering of the poor, so scattering those birds would have cost the poorest people in the court their sacrifice (John 2:15-16).

"My Father's house" is the first claim He makes in this Gospel, and it is a claim about sonship as much as about trading. Luke has Him using almost the same words at twelve years old (John 2:16, Luke 2:49).
The disciples remember Psalm 69, which is quoted more often in the New Testament than almost any other psalm, and always about suffering (John 2:17).
"Destroy this temple" is an imperative. He is not proposing it; He is telling them what they are going to do (John 2:19).
Forty-six years puts the conversation around AD 27 or 28, since Herod's rebuilding began around 20 BC. It is one of the firmest chronological pegs in the Gospels (John 2:20).
Verse 21 is John's own note, added long afterwards - he spoke of the temple of his body - and verse 22 admits that nobody understood it at the time (John 2:21-22).

The last three verses are a warning attached to a success. Many believed when they saw the signs, and He did not entrust Himself to them. It is the same verb both ways: they believed in Him, and He did not believe in them (John 2:23-24).
"He knew what was in man" closes the chapter - and the next word in the Gospel is Nicodemus, a man arriving with a carefully prepared opening line (John 2:25, 3:1).

intro: A wedding in a village nobody has heard of, and the catering fails. A village wedding was the party of the decade and ran for days; running out of wine was not an inconvenience but a humiliation the town would still be discussing in twenty years. His mother comes to Him and says four words. They have no wine. She does not ask for anything - she simply tells Him.

The reply sounds cold in English. Woman is not rude in Greek, and He uses the same address to her from the cross, but it is not mother either, and the distance in it is real. What does that have to do with you and me is an old Hebrew idiom, found in Samuel and in Kings, meaning this is not a matter we share. And my hour has not yet come starts a clock that runs the length of this Gospel; when the hour finally arrives, it is the cross. Her answer is to turn to the servants and say whatever He tells you, do it - the last words Mary speaks anywhere in Scripture.

Six stone jars, and the detail earns its place twice over. Stone, because stone cannot contract ritual impurity, which is exactly why the water for purification was kept in it. And six rather than seven. Something like a hundred and twenty gallons of washing water, filled to the brim and turned into the wine of a wedding feast. Nothing is smashed and nobody is lectured about ceremony; the same vessels are filled and put to a better use. And no one sees it happen - there is no gesture and no word spoken over the water, only a servant dipping a cup. The master of the feast does not know where it came from, and the servants who drew it do. That will keep happening in this book: the people who did what they were told are the people who know.

The compliment goes to a bridegroom who had nothing to do with it, which is quietly funny and also a set-up, because the next chapter identifies who the bridegroom actually is. And John calls this the beginning of the signs - not a mighty work, which is the word the other Gospels reach for, but a sign, which points away from itself.

Then Jerusalem and the tables. Matthew, Mark and Luke all place this in the final week and John places it at the beginning: either it happened twice, three years apart, or John has set it here for reasons of theme. Serious readers hold both and this book does not pretend to settle it. What He does is worth watching closely. The whip, which only John mentions, is used on the animals; to the men selling doves He speaks instead, and doves were the offering of the poor, so loosing those birds would have cost the poorest people in the court what they came with. Even overturning the place, He is careful about who pays. And what He calls it is the first claim He makes in this Gospel - my Father's house. Destroy this temple is an imperative, not a proposal; He is telling them what they will do. Forty-six years of building sets the conversation around AD 27 or 28, and John adds, long afterwards, that He spoke of the temple of His body, and that nobody understood it until He was raised. The chapter ends on a warning attached to a success: many believed when they saw the signs, and He did not entrust Himself to them. It is the same verb both ways. They believed in Him; He did not believe in them.

verses.1: The third day, there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there.
verses.2: Jesus also was invited, with his disciples, to the marriage.
verses.3: When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to him, “They have no wine.”
verses.4: Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour has not yet come.”
verses.5: His mother said to the servants, “Whatever he says to you, do it.”
verses.6: Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying, containing two or three metretes apiece.
verses.7: Jesus said to them, “Fill the water pots with water.” They filled them up to the brim.
verses.8: He said to them, “Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast.” So they took it.
verses.9: When the ruler of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and didn’t know where it came from (but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the ruler of the feast called the bridegroom,
verses.10: and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, then that which is worse. You have kept the good wine until now!”
verses.11: This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
verses.12: After this, he went down to Capernaum, he, and his mother, his brothers, and his disciples; and they stayed there a few days.
verses.13: The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
verses.14: He found in the temple those who sold oxen, sheep, and doves, and the changers of money sitting.
verses.15: He made a whip of cords, and threw all out of the temple, both the sheep and the oxen; and he poured out the changers’ money, and overthrew their tables.
verses.16: To those who sold the doves, he said, “Take these things out of here! Don’t make my Father’s house a marketplace!”
verses.17: His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will eat me up.”
verses.18: The Jews therefore answered him, “What sign do you show us, seeing that you do these things?”
verses.19: Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
verses.20: The Jews therefore said, “It took forty-six years to build this temple! Will you raise it up in three days?”
verses.21: But he spoke of the temple of his body.
verses.22: When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he said this, and they believed the Scripture, and the word which Jesus had said.
verses.23: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the feast, many believed in his name, observing his signs which he did.
verses.24: But Jesus didn’t entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone,
verses.25: and because he didn’t need for anyone to testify concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 3 - Born From Above, a Serpent Lifted in the Wilderness, and He Must Increase
chapters.title: Born From Above, a Serpent Lifted in the Wilderness, and He Must Increase
keyNotes: The chapter break hides a joint. Chapter 2 ends with He knew what was in man, and the next sentence introduces a man with a carefully prepared opening line (John 3:1, 2:25).
Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a ruler - which means the Sanhedrin - and in verse 10 he is called the teacher of Israel, with the article. He is not a curious layman (John 3:1, 10).

He comes at night. In a Gospel that runs on light and darkness, the detail is not neutral - and Nicodemus appears twice more, the last time in daylight with seventy-five pounds of spices for a burial (John 3:2, 7:50, 19:39).
"We know" is plural. He is speaking for other people who have reached the same conclusion and have not said so out loud (John 3:2).

The word behind born anew is anothen, which means both again and from above. Nicodemus hears the first; Yahshua means the second; and the whole exchange runs on the ambiguity. It works in Greek and not in Aramaic, which raises a fair question about what language this conversation was held in. The text does not answer it (John 3:3-4).

"Born of water and spirit" has been read as natural birth then spiritual birth, as baptism, and as Ezekiel 36 - I will sprinkle clean water on you, and I will put my Spirit within you. The last of those is a passage the teacher of Israel would be expected to know, which fits the rebuke that follows (John 3:5, 10).
Wind and spirit are one word in Greek, and one word in Hebrew too. The saying only works because they are the same word (John 3:8).
"You hear its sound but don't know where it comes from" - the wind is known by its effects and not by its origin, and so is everyone born of the Spirit (John 3:8).

"Are you the teacher of Israel and don't understand these things?" assumes the new birth was already there in the Hebrew Scriptures to be understood. He is not being told he missed a new doctrine; he is being told he missed his own (John 3:10).
"Who is in heaven" at the end of verse 13 is present in many manuscripts and absent from others. The WEB prints it (John 3:13).

The bronze serpent is Numbers 21. The people are dying of snakebite, and what God tells Moses to lift up is a snake - an image of the very thing killing them. They are not healed by looking away but by looking at it (John 3:14).
That serpent later had to be destroyed, because Israel started burning incense to it. The cure became an idol within a few centuries (John 3:14, 2 Kings 18:4).
"Lifted up" is hypsoo, and in this Gospel it always carries both meanings at once - lifted onto a cross, and lifted into glory. He never separates them (John 3:14, 8:28, 12:32).
"God so loved the world" is houtos - in this way, in this manner. The verse is about how God loved, not only how much (John 3:16).
"One and only" is monogenes - unique, one of a kind. It is a statement about there being no second, rather than about origin (John 3:16, 18).
The judgment in verse 19 is not a sentence handed down but a preference already exercised: the light came, and men loved the darkness. The verdict is what people did with it (John 3:19).

Where the quotation ends is a real question. The Greek has no quotation marks, and verse 15 and verse 21 are both defensible as the last words spoken to Nicodemus. The WEB closes it at 21 (John 3:15-21).
"Jesus baptized" in verse 22 is corrected a chapter later, where John notes that in fact His disciples did the baptizing, not He Himself (John 3:22, 4:2).
Enon near Salim, because there was much water there, is the kind of detail a traveller remembers and a theologian would not invent (John 3:23).
"For John was not yet thrown into prison" is a quiet correction of the impression the other Gospels leave, where John's arrest comes before the ministry begins (John 3:24).

The friend of the bridegroom was a real office - he arranged the marriage, made the negotiations, and stood aside on the day. His whole joy is in hearing the bridegroom's voice, which means his success is his own redundancy (John 3:29).
"He must increase, but I must decrease" is the last thing John the Baptist says in this Gospel. He goes out on a sentence about becoming smaller (John 3:30).
Whether verses 31 to 36 are still John speaking or the writer's own commentary is disputed, and the text gives no marker either way (John 3:31-36).
"The wrath of God remains on him" is a present continuous verb. The wrath is not described as arriving later; it is described as already resting, and belief is what lifts it (John 3:36).

intro: The chapter break hides a joint. Chapter 2 closes with the note that He knew what was in man, and the next sentence introduces a man arriving with a carefully prepared opening line. Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a ruler - which means the Sanhedrin - and a few verses later he is called the teacher of Israel, with the article. He is not a curious layman. And his we know is plural: he speaks for people who have reached a conclusion privately and are not saying so in daylight, which is why he comes at night, in a book that runs on light and dark from its first page. Though he should not be dismissed too quickly, because he appears twice more, and the last time it is in the open, at a Roman cross, carrying seventy-five pounds of burial spices while the disciples are in hiding.

The compliment is not answered. Unless one is born anothen, he cannot see the Kingdom - and the word means both again and from above. Nicodemus hears the first, which makes his question literal rather than stupid, and the whole conversation runs on the double meaning. Born of water and spirit has been read as natural birth followed by spiritual, and as baptism, but the rebuke that follows points elsewhere: are you the teacher of Israel and do not understand these things? That only makes sense if the answer was already in the book he taught from - and it is. Ezekiel promises clean water sprinkled and a new spirit put within. He is not being told he missed a new doctrine. He is being told he missed his own Scriptures.

The wind saying works only because wind and spirit are one word, in Greek and in Hebrew alike. The wind is known by what it moves rather than by where it started, and so is everyone born of the Spirit.

Then the strangest picture in the chapter. In Numbers the people are dying of snakebite, and what God tells Moses to raise on a pole is a snake - an image of the very thing killing them. They are not healed by looking away but by looking straight at it. There is a footnote to that story worth carrying: centuries later Israel was burning incense to the bronze serpent and Hezekiah had to destroy it, because the cure had become an idol. And lifted up in this Gospel always carries both senses at once - raised on a cross and raised into glory. John never separates them; in this book the cross is the throne.

Then the verse familiarity has sanded smooth. God so loved the world does not mean so much; the Greek means in this way, in this manner, and it points back at the serpent. This is how God loved - He lifted His Son where everyone dying could see Him. And the judgment that follows is not a sentence handed down but a preference already exercised: the light came, and men loved the darkness. The chapter closes with one of the most dignified paragraphs in Scripture. John's disciples come to him hurt, watching their teacher's work drain away, and he answers with the picture of the shoshbin - the friend of the bridegroom, who arranged the marriage, did the negotiating, ran the day, and then stood outside the chamber and was glad to hear the bridegroom's voice. The friend's success is his own redundancy. He must increase, but I must decrease are the last words John the Baptist speaks in this Gospel. He is given no farewell scene. He goes out on a sentence about becoming smaller.

verses.1: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.
verses.2: The same came to him by night, and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.”
verses.3: Jesus answered him, “Most certainly, I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.”
verses.4: Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb, and be born?”
verses.5: Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom.
verses.6: That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
verses.7: Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born anew.’
verses.8: The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”
verses.9: Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things be?”
verses.10: Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things?
verses.11: Most certainly I tell you, we speak that which we know, and testify of that which we have seen, and you don’t receive our witness.
verses.12: If I told you earthly things and you don’t believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?
verses.13: No one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.
verses.14: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up,
verses.15: that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
verses.16: For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
verses.17: For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
verses.18: He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the one and only Son of God.
verses.19: This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light; for their works were evil.
verses.20: For everyone who does evil hates the light, and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed.
verses.21: But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God.”
verses.22: After these things, Jesus came with his disciples into the land of Judea. He stayed there with them, and baptized.
verses.23: John also was baptizing in Enon near Salim, because there was much water there. They came, and were baptized.
verses.24: For John was not yet thrown into prison.
verses.25: There arose therefore a questioning on the part of John’s disciples with some Jews about purification.
verses.26: They came to John, and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, the same baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.”
verses.27: John answered, “A man can receive nothing, unless it has been given him from heaven.
verses.28: You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’
verses.29: He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.
verses.30: He must increase, but I must decrease.
verses.31: He who comes from above is above all. He who is from the earth belongs to the earth, and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all.
verses.32: What he has seen and heard, of that he testifies; and no one receives his witness.
verses.33: He who has received his witness has set his seal to this, that God is true.
verses.34: For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for God gives the Spirit without measure.
verses.35: The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.
verses.36: One who believes in the Son has eternal life, but one who disobeys the Son won’t see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.”

Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your offspring, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 4 - A Tired Man at a Well, Living Water, and a Word That Healed From Twenty Miles
chapters.title: A Tired Man at a Well, Living Water, and a Word That Healed From Twenty Miles
keyNotes: Yahshua Himself did not baptize; His disciples did. John stops to correct the rumor in the middle of a sentence (John 4:1-2).

"He needed to pass through Samaria" uses the same small verb John uses for the Son of Man who must be lifted up and the friend who must decrease. The road through Samaria was the shortest way north, but in this Gospel that word usually means more than geography (John 4:4, 3:14, 3:30).
Sychar sits near the ground Jacob gave to Joseph, and Joseph's bones were buried at Shechem in that same field. This conversation happens on family land (John 4:5, Genesis 48:22, Joshua 24:32).
He was tired. The Word who made all things got worn out walking and sat down on the edge of a well. John does not let the reader forget the flesh (John 4:6).

"About the sixth hour" counts from sunrise, so about noon - the heat of the day, when water was not usually drawn. Some readers take it as Roman reckoning from midnight, which would make it six in the evening. Either way John wants the hour remembered (John 4:6, 19:14).

A man and a woman meeting at a well is one of the oldest scenes in Scripture. Abraham's servant found Rebekah at a well, Jacob met Rachel at one, Moses met Zipporah at one. Every time it leads to a marriage. And John has just finished calling Yahshua the bridegroom (John 4:7, 3:29, Genesis 24:11-14, 29:9-11).
"Jews have no dealings with Samaritans" may be narrower in the Greek - they do not share vessels. Which is exactly what He has just asked to do. He wants a drink from her jar (John 4:9).

The Samaritans traced back to the peoples the king of Assyria settled in the land after the northern kingdom fell, who feared Yahweh and served their own gods at the same time. Seven hundred years later the wound was still open (John 4:9, 2 Kings 17:24, 33).

"Living water" in ordinary speech meant running water, from a spring, as opposed to water standing in a cistern. She hears plumbing. He means what Jeremiah meant when Yahweh called Himself the spring of living waters (John 4:10-11, Jeremiah 2:13).

"Are you greater than our father Jacob?" is the first of two such questions in John. Four chapters later someone asks if He is greater than Abraham. Both times the honest answer is yes (John 4:12, 8:53).
"A spring of water welling up" uses a verb for leaping or springing up. The water He gives does not sit still in a person (John 4:14).

He does not shame her and He does not skip it. Go, call your husband. She answers with a half-truth, and He tells her it is true and fills in the other half. That is the whole conversation about her past (John 4:16-18).

Some readers see the five husbands as a picture of Samaria's history, since the king of Assyria brought in peoples from five cities. It is a possible echo. The text gives no sign that she is anything but a real woman with a real history (John 4:18, 2 Kings 17:24).

"This mountain" is Gerizim, where Moses had the blessing proclaimed, and where the Samaritans built their own temple. It had been destroyed by a Jewish king more than a century before this conversation, and they still worshipped on the ruins (John 4:20, Deuteronomy 11:29).
He takes a side - salvation is from the Jews - and in the same breath says the side is about to stop mattering. The hour is coming when neither mountain will be the place (John 4:21-22).

"In spirit and truth" is not inward instead of real. It is worship that answers to who God actually is. And the line most people skip: the Father is seeking such people. Worship is something He is looking for (John 4:23-24).

The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses, so the Messiah they waited for was the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18. She expects someone who will tell them everything (John 4:25, Deuteronomy 18:18).
"I am he" is two words in Greek: ego eimi, I am. It is the first time in the Gospel He says it, and He says it to a Samaritan woman at noon (John 4:26).
She left her water jar. She had come to draw water, and she forgot it, which tells you what kind of conversation it was (John 4:28).
"Come, see a man who told me everything that I did" is the same invitation Philip gave Nathanael. Come and see. She becomes the first person in John to bring a whole town (John 4:29, 1:46).
"My food is to do the will of him who sent me." The disciples went to buy lunch. He had already eaten (John 4:32-34).
Four months from sowing to harvest was a farmer's saying. He tells them to look up, and what they would have seen coming down the road from Sychar was a crowd of Samaritans (John 4:35, 4:30).
"Savior of the world" is said in the New Testament only here and in John's first letter. The first people in this Gospel to say it are Samaritans (John 4:42, 1 John 4:14).
A prophet has no honor in his own country. The other Gospels use the saying of Nazareth. John places it here, as He heads back into Galilee (John 4:44).
The nobleman is a royal official, likely in the service of Herod Antipas. Cana to Capernaum is about twenty miles, uphill all the way from the lake. He walked it to ask (John 4:46-47).
"Unless you see signs and wonders" is plural - you all. It is spoken to the crowd as much as to the father (John 4:48).
"The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way." He believed before anything happened. The servants met him on the road the next day with the news (John 4:50-51).
The fever left at the seventh hour, the very hour the word was spoken, from twenty miles away. Distance did not slow the word down (John 4:52-53, Psalm 107:20).
John numbers the first two signs, both at Cana, and then stops counting. From here the reader is trusted to keep track (John 4:54, 2:11).

intro: The chapter opens with the Word made flesh too tired to keep walking. It is about noon, the disciples have gone into Sychar for food, and Yahshua sits down on the edge of Jacob's well, on the land Jacob gave to Joseph. A woman comes out alone to draw water in the heat of the day, when no one draws water - the hour for someone who does not want to be talked about. And He asks her for a drink, which crosses three lines at once: Jew and Samaritan, man and woman, and a rabbi drinking from a Samaritan's jar.

He offers living water, and she hears the ordinary meaning, running spring water rather than the still water of a cistern. Asked whether He is greater than Jacob, He answers by contrasting the two waters: one that leaves a person thirsty again, and one that becomes a spring leaping up inside. She asks for it so that she will never have to come back to this well, still thinking about the walk at noon. Then He tells her to call her husband, and when she says she has none, He agrees with her and supplies what she left out. He neither shames her nor skips it.

She turns the conversation to the question of where worship belongs, Gerizim or Jerusalem, and He answers it honestly. Salvation is from the Jews; and yet the hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. The line at the center of the chapter is that the Father is seeking such people. When she speaks of the Messiah who will tell them everything, He says ego eimi - I am, the one speaking to you - the first time the phrase is spoken in John, and it is spoken to her.

She leaves her water jar and goes back into the town she had been avoiding, telling everyone to come and see a man who told her everything she ever did. The disciples urge Him to eat; He says His food is to do the will of the one who sent Him, and tells them to lift their eyes, because the fields are already white - and what is coming down the road from Sychar is a crowd of Samaritans, who end by calling Him the Savior of the world. Then in Galilee a royal official walks twenty miles to beg for his dying son and is sent home with a sentence: go, your son lives. He believes the word before he sees anything, and his servants meet him on the road. The fever left at the very hour the word was spoken.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 5 - Thirty-Eight Years by the Pool, a Mat on the Sabbath, and the Witnesses Called to the Stand
chapters.title: Thirty-Eight Years by the Pool, a Mat on the Sabbath, and the Witnesses Called to the Stand
keyNotes: The feast is not named. Readers have argued for Passover, Purim, Pentecost and Tabernacles. John names nearly every other feast he mentions, so the silence may simply mean the feast is not the point (John 5:1).
The sheep gate was the gate the priests rebuilt and sanctified in Nehemiah's day, near the temple, where animals for sacrifice came in (John 5:2, Nehemiah 3:1).

Five porches around a pool sounded like legend to some readers for centuries. Excavations near the church of St Anne in Jerusalem uncovered a double pool with colonnades on four sides and a fifth across the middle (John 5:2).

The end of verse 3 and all of verse 4, the angel stirring the water, are missing from the earliest manuscripts and are printed in the WEB. Whether John wrote them or a later copyist explained the scene, verse 7 shows that this is what the sick people believed (John 5:3-4, 5:7).

Thirty-eight years is precisely the time Israel spent between Kadesh Barnea and the brook Zered, until the whole generation that refused to go in had died. John gives the number without comment (John 5:5, Deuteronomy 2:14).
"Do you want to be made well?" is a real question, not a cruel one. Some people have built a whole life around what is wrong with them (John 5:6).
He never says yes. He explains why nobody helps him and someone always beats him to it. The answer to a question about wanting is a story about other people (John 5:7).
"Arise, take up your mat, and walk" is almost word for word what Yahshua says about the paralyzed man let down through the roof in Mark. The mat was a poor man's bedroll (John 5:8, Mark 2:9).
There is no faith required of him in the story. He does not know who healed him and cannot point Him out. Grace in this chapter goes first and asks questions later (John 5:13).
"It was the Sabbath on that day" is withheld until after the healing, which is how John makes the reader feel the turn (John 5:9).

Jeremiah 17 does forbid carrying a burden out of the house on the Sabbath, and Nehemiah shut the gates against the traders' loads. The man's mat was his own bed, and his accusers never once ask about what had just happened to him. Yahshua does not answer with a ruling on carrying at all. He answers with who His Father is (John 5:10, 5:17, Jeremiah 17:21-22).

"Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you" links this man's past to his condition in a way Yahshua refuses to do for the man born blind four chapters later. Not all suffering comes from sin. Some does (John 5:14, 9:3).
The healed man goes straight to the authorities with the name. Whether from fear or gratitude, the text does not say, and it is fair to notice that he never thanks anyone (John 5:15).

"My Father is still working, so I am working too." God rested from creating on the seventh day, but He never stopped holding the world together, giving life and receiving the dead. Yahshua claims to be doing what His Father does on the Sabbath (John 5:17, Psalm 121:4).
They understood Him perfectly. Calling God His own Father in that sense was making Himself equal with God. Nobody in the scene thinks He is claiming to be merely a good man (John 5:18, 10:33).
"The Son can do nothing of himself" is not weakness. It is the reverse - whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. Total dependence and total equality in the same breath (John 5:19).
Giving life to the dead and judging the world were the two things the Hebrew Scriptures reserve for God alone. He claims both in four verses (John 5:21-22, Deuteronomy 32:39).
"Honor the Son, even as they honor the Father." The same honor, not a lesser one (John 5:23).
"Has eternal life" and "has passed out of death into life" are present and past. It is not only something waiting at the end (John 5:24).

"Because he is a son of man" is the only place in the Gospels where the phrase has no article at all - not the Son of Man, but a son of man - which is exactly how Daniel 7 puts it (John 5:27, Daniel 7:13).

"All who are in the tombs will hear his voice" is the clearest echo in the Gospels of Daniel 12:2 - two resurrections, one to life and one to judgment, and both come out of the grave at His voice (John 5:28-29, Daniel 12:2).

A witness who speaks only for himself was not enough under the Torah. Every matter is established by two or three witnesses, so He calls four: John, His own works, the Father, and the Scriptures (John 5:31-39, Deuteronomy 19:15).
John was "the burning and shining lamp" - a lamp, not the light. The same distinction the prologue made (John 5:35, 1:8).
"You search the Scriptures" can be read as a command or a statement, and either works. The point lands the same: they read the right book and missed who it was about (John 5:39-40).
"If another comes in his own name, you will receive him." History is full of men who did, and were (John 5:43).
The final witness for the prosecution is Moses. The one they claimed as theirs is the one who wrote about Him (John 5:45-47, Deuteronomy 18:15).

intro: By the sheep gate in Jerusalem lies a pool with five porches, and every porch is crowded with the sick, all watching the water. The note in verse 4 about an angel stirring it is missing from the earliest manuscripts, but whoever wrote it, verse 7 confirms that this is what the people lying there believed. One man has lain there thirty-eight years - exactly the span Israel spent between Kadesh Barnea and the brook Zered, until the generation that refused to enter the land had died. John supplies the number without comment.

Yahshua picks out one man and asks whether he wants to be made well. The man never says yes. He explains that he has no one to help him and that someone always gets there first. Thirty-eight years will build a life around what is wrong, and the question is less cruel than it sounds. Without waiting for a better answer, Yahshua tells him to rise, take up his mat and walk, and he does. Only then does John add that it was the Sabbath.

The first words spoken to a man who has not walked in thirty-eight years concern the bed he is carrying. To be fair to the accusers, Jeremiah 17 does forbid carrying a burden out of the house on the Sabbath. But no one asks what has happened to him and no one rejoices; they step past the miracle to reach the mat. And Yahshua does not answer with a ruling on carrying. He says that His Father is working still, and so is He. God rested from creating, but He has never stopped sustaining the world, and the one who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. His hearers understood Him exactly, and wanted Him dead for making Himself equal with God.

He does not retreat. The Son gives life to whom He wills; all judgment has been given to Him; all should honor the Son as they honor the Father. Giving life and judging the world are the two works the Hebrew Scriptures reserve for God, and He claims both, along with the hour when all who are in the tombs will hear His voice and come out, as Daniel 12 foresaw. Then, because the Torah requires two or three witnesses, He calls four: John, His works, the Father, and the Scriptures, which they search without coming to the one they testify about. The last witness is Moses, the man they counted as theirs, who wrote about Him.

verses.1: After these things, there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
verses.2: Now in Jerusalem by the sheep gate, there is a pool, which is called in Hebrew, “Bethesda”, having five porches.
verses.3: In these lay a great multitude of those who were sick, blind, lame, or paralyzed, waiting for the moving of the water;
verses.4: for an angel went down at certain times into the pool, and stirred up the water. Whoever stepped in first after the stirring of the water was healed of whatever disease he had.
verses.5: A certain man was there, who had been sick for thirty-eight years.
verses.6: When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had been sick for a long time, he asked him, “Do you want to be made well?”
verses.7: The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, but while I’m coming, another steps down before me.”
verses.8: Jesus said to him, “Arise, take up your mat, and walk.”
verses.9: Immediately, the man was made well, and took up his mat and walked. Now it was the Sabbath on that day.
verses.10: So the Jews said to him who was cured, “It is the Sabbath. It is not lawful for you to carry the mat.”
verses.11: He answered them, “He who made me well, the same said to me, ‘Take up your mat, and walk.’”
verses.12: Then they asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ‘Take up your mat, and walk’?”
verses.13: But he who was healed didn’t know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, a crowd being in the place.
verses.14: Afterward Jesus found him in the temple, and said to him, “Behold, you are made well. Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you.”
verses.15: The man went away, and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.
verses.16: For this cause the Jews persecuted Jesus, and sought to kill him, because he did these things on the Sabbath.
verses.17: But Jesus answered them, “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.”
verses.18: For this cause therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God.
verses.19: Jesus therefore answered them, “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.
verses.20: For the Father has affection for the Son, and shows him all things that he himself does. He will show him greater works than these, that you may marvel.
verses.21: For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life to whom he desires.
verses.22: For the Father judges no one, but he has given all judgment to the Son,
verses.23: that all may honor the Son, even as they honor the Father. He who doesn’t honor the Son doesn’t honor the Father who sent him.
verses.24: “Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word, and believes him who sent me, has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life.
verses.25: Most certainly, I tell you, the hour comes, and now is, when the dead will hear the Son of God’s voice; and those who hear will live.
verses.26: For as the Father has life in himself, even so he gave to the Son also to have life in himself.
verses.27: He also gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is a son of man.
verses.28: Don’t marvel at this, for the hour comes, in which all that are in the tombs will hear his voice,
verses.29: and will come out; those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.
verses.30: I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.
verses.31: “If I testify about myself, my witness is not valid.
verses.32: It is another who testifies about me. I know that the testimony which he testifies about me is true.
verses.33: You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth.
verses.34: But the testimony which I receive is not from man. However, I say these things that you may be saved.
verses.35: He was the burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.
verses.36: But the testimony which I have is greater than that of John, for the works which the Father gave me to accomplish, the very works that I do, testify about me, that the Father has sent me.
verses.37: The Father himself, who sent me, has testified about me. You have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his form.
verses.38: You don’t have his word living in you; because you don’t believe him whom he sent.
verses.39: “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me.
verses.40: Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.
verses.41: I don’t receive glory from men.
verses.42: But I know you, that you don’t have God’s love in yourselves.
verses.43: I have come in my Father’s name, and you don’t receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.
verses.44: How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God?
verses.45: “Don’t think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you, even Moses, on whom you have set your hope.
verses.46: For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote about me.
verses.47: But if you don’t believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 6 - Five Barley Loaves, I AM on the Water, and the Bread That Came Down From Heaven
chapters.title: Five Barley Loaves, I AM on the Water, and the Bread That Came Down From Heaven
keyNotes: John alone calls the lake the Sea of Tiberias, after the city Herod Antipas built on its shore and named for the emperor. His readers knew it by that name (John 6:1, 21:1).

"The Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand." This is the second Passover John marks, and everything in the chapter happens in its shadow: bread, a crossing of water, and manna in the wilderness (John 6:4, 2:13, 11:55).

He asks Philip where to buy bread, and John adds that He already knew what He would do. Philip was from Bethsaida, the nearest town. It was a test, and Philip answers it with arithmetic (John 6:5-7, 1:44).
Two hundred denarii was about two hundred days' wages for a laborer, most of a year's pay, and Philip says it would not be enough for everyone to get a little (John 6:7, Matthew 20:2).
Moses asked almost the same question in the wilderness. Where could I get meat to give all these people? Would all the fish of the sea be enough? (John 6:5, Numbers 11:13, 11:22).

Only John says the loaves were barley, the cheap bread of the poor, and only John mentions the boy who had them. Elisha once fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves and had some left over (John 6:9, 2 Kings 4:42-44).
"There was much grass in the place" - spring, as Passover would be. Mark says green grass. Small details like this are how eyewitness memory reads (John 6:10, Mark 6:39).

"Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost." The same word, lost, is used about two dozen verses later for the people the Father gives Him: of all He has given Me, I should lose nothing (John 6:12, 6:39).
Twelve baskets left - one for each of the twelve who had just watched the arithmetic fail (John 6:13).

"This is truly the prophet who comes into the world" is the prophet like Moses of Deuteronomy 18. They had just watched bread appear in the wilderness, which is exactly what you would expect a new Moses to do (John 6:14, Deuteronomy 18:15).
They wanted to take Him by force and make Him king. He withdrew to the mountain alone. A crown offered by a full stomach is not the kingdom (John 6:15).
Twenty-five or thirty stadia is three or four miles - the middle of the lake, at night, rowing into the wind (John 6:19).

In the Hebrew Scriptures the one who walks on the waves of the sea is God. Job says He alone treads on them. The psalm says His way was through the sea and His footsteps were not seen (John 6:19, Job 9:8, Psalm 77:19).
"It is I" is ego eimi again, the same two words He spoke to the woman at the well. On the water in the dark they carry their full weight: I AM. Don't be afraid (John 6:20, 4:26).
"Immediately the boat was at the land where they were going." John gives no explanation and does not need one (John 6:21, Psalm 107:30).
"You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves." They had the bread and missed the sign. The bread was the point to them; it was the pointer to Him (John 6:26).
"Him the Father, God, has sealed" uses the image of a seal pressed into wax, the mark that proves who owns or sent something (John 6:27).
What must we do to do the works of God? The answer is one work, singular: believe in the one He sent (John 6:28-29).
They ask for a sign after watching five thousand eat. Then they quote the manna. Moses gave our fathers bread from heaven. They are asking Him to top it (John 6:30-31, Psalm 78:24).
He corrects three things in one sentence: it was not Moses, it was My Father; not gave, but gives; and the true bread is not something but someone (John 6:32-33).
"I am the bread of life" is the first of seven I AM sayings with a picture attached: bread, light, door, good shepherd, resurrection, way, vine (John 6:35, 8:12, 10:9, 10:11, 11:25, 14:6, 15:1).
"Him who comes to me I will in no way throw out." The Greek doubles the negative. Never, under any circumstances (John 6:37).
"I will raise him up at the last day" is said four times in this chapter. Whatever else this bread means, it ends in resurrection (John 6:39, 40, 44, 54).
The Jews murmured, which is the wilderness word. Israel murmured against Moses over the bread, and Moses told them their murmuring was against Yahweh (John 6:41, Exodus 16:8).
"They will all be taught by God" is Isaiah 54. The drawing of the Father is not a feeling but a teaching, and those who learn come (John 6:44-45, Isaiah 54:13).
From verse 54 on, the verb for eat changes to one that means to chew or gnaw. He does not soften the image when they object. He makes it harder (John 6:54-58).

Drinking blood was forbidden from Noah onward, because the life is in the blood. To a Jewish ear this is the most offensive thing He could say - unless He is saying that His life is the life given for theirs (John 6:53, Leviticus 17:11).
"The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life." The way into the hard saying is through the words, not around them (John 6:63).
Many of His disciples turned back and walked with Him no more. They did not stop believing in God. They stopped walking with Him (John 6:66).
"You have the words of eternal life" is the answer to the words that drove everyone else away. Peter does not say he understands. He says there is nowhere else to go (John 6:68).
"The Holy One of God" is the title a demon shouted in the synagogue at Capernaum. Here a disciple says it on purpose (John 6:69, Mark 1:24).
He chose twelve and one of them is a devil. Judas was chosen too, and stayed through all of it (John 6:70-71).

intro: Passover is near, and the chapter moves through the shape of the Exodus: bread in the wilderness, a crossing of water, murmuring, and manna. A great crowd follows Yahshua around the lake, and He asks Philip where they could buy bread for them all, knowing already what He would do. Philip answers the test with arithmetic - two hundred denarii, most of a year's wages, would not give everyone a bite - the same despairing sum Moses did in the wilderness when he asked where he could find meat for all the people. Andrew finds a boy with five barley loaves, the bread of the poor, and two fish, and asks what that could be among so many.

The people sit down on the spring grass, five thousand men, and eat as much as they want. Then comes the command to gather the fragments so that nothing is lost - the same word He will use of the people the Father gives Him, of whom He will lose nothing. The way He treats bread is the way He treats people. Twelve baskets remain. The crowd rightly recognises the prophet like Moses and then tries to seize Him and make Him king, and He withdraws alone to the mountain rather than accept a crown from people whose stomachs are full.

That night the disciples, rowing into a storm in the middle of the lake, see Him walking on the sea, which in the Hebrew Scriptures is what God alone does. He calls out ego eimi - it is I, and for anyone who knows the burning bush, I AM - and the moment they take Him aboard they reach the shore. The next day the crowd finds Him and He tells them plainly that they came for the bread, not the sign. They ask for a sign anyway and invoke the manna, and He answers that it was never Moses who gave bread from heaven, that His Father gives the true bread, and that He is that bread.

They murmur, as their fathers did, and instead of softening the saying He sharpens it: unless they eat His flesh and drink His blood they have no life in them. Blood was forbidden from Noah onward because the life is in the blood, and that is exactly the point - He is offering His life for theirs. When they object He changes the verb to one that means to chew. Many disciples turn back, and He asks the twelve whether they will go too. Peter does not claim to understand. He says there is nowhere else to go, because Yahshua has the words of eternal life.

verses.1: After these things, Jesus went away to the other side of the sea of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias.
verses.2: A great multitude followed him, because they saw his signs which he did on those who were sick.
verses.3: Jesus went up into the mountain, and he sat there with his disciples.
verses.4: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.
verses.5: Jesus therefore lifting up his eyes, and seeing that a great multitude was coming to him, said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, that these may eat?”
verses.6: This he said to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.
verses.7: Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not sufficient for them, that everyone of them may receive a little.”
verses.8: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,
verses.9: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?”
verses.10: Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in that place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand.
verses.11: Jesus took the loaves; and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down; likewise also of the fish as much as they desired.
verses.12: When they were filled, he said to his disciples, “Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost.”
verses.13: So they gathered them up, and filled twelve baskets with broken pieces from the five barley loaves, which were left over by those who had eaten.
verses.14: When therefore the people saw the sign which Jesus did, they said, “This is truly the prophet who comes into the world.”
verses.15: Jesus therefore, perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force, to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
verses.16: When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea,
verses.17: and they entered into the boat, and were going over the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not come to them.
verses.18: The sea was tossed by a great wind blowing.
verses.19: When therefore they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing near to the boat; and they were afraid.
verses.20: But he said to them, “It is I. Don’t be afraid.”
verses.21: They were willing therefore to receive him into the boat. Immediately the boat was at the land where they were going.
