chapters.heading: CHAPTER 7 - Brothers Who Did Not Believe, a Shout on the Last Day, and Rivers of Living Water
chapters.title: Brothers Who Did Not Believe, a Shout on the Last Day, and Rivers of Living Water
keyNotes: He stayed in Galilee because the Judeans were looking to kill Him. Chapter 5 ended with a death plot, and it is still in the air (John 7:1, 5:18).

Tabernacles was the feast of tents, seven days of rejoicing after the harvest was in, with the whole household - servants, foreigners, widows and orphans included - living in booths. It was the most crowded week of the year in Jerusalem (John 7:2, Leviticus 23:34, Deuteronomy 16:13-14).

"Even his brothers didn't believe in him." These are the brothers who grew up in the same house. One of them, James, later led the assembly in Jerusalem and wrote a letter in the New Testament. Unbelief at the dinner table is not the end of the story (John 7:5, 1 Corinthians 15:7).

Their advice is pure public relations: nobody does things in secret if he wants to be known, so show yourself to the world. It is the same logic as the wilderness temptation - prove it in public (John 7:3-4).

"My time has not yet come" is a different word from "my hour." It means the right moment, the opportune season. Theirs, He says, is always ready, because nothing they do costs them anything (John 7:6).

"I am not yet going up to this feast" - and then He goes. Some manuscripts read "not yet," others simply "not." Either way He refuses to go on their terms, as a public show, and goes later on His own (John 7:8-10).
The crowd murmurs, which is the wilderness word again, and is split between "he is a good man" and "he leads the multitude astray." Nobody says it out loud, for fear (John 7:12-13).

"How does this man know letters, having never been educated?" He had not studied under a recognised rabbi. They meant: where did He get His authority? He answers: from the one who sent Me (John 7:15-16).
"If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching." Obedience comes before understanding here, not after it. You find out whether it is true by being willing to do it (John 7:17).
"Didn't Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law?" He is not attacking the Torah. He is accusing them of breaking it, by plotting murder while defending the Sabbath (John 7:19).

Circumcision on the eighth day went ahead even when the eighth day fell on a Sabbath, because the instruction about the eighth day came first. His argument: if you can perform a covenant act on one part of a man on the Sabbath, why be angry that I made the whole man well? (John 7:22-23, Leviticus 12:3).
"Don't judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment" is almost a quotation of Deuteronomy 16, the charge given to every judge in Israel (John 7:24, Deuteronomy 16:18).

"When the Christ comes, no one will know where he comes from" reflects an expectation that the Messiah would appear suddenly and unknown. They think they know where He is from. They are only half right (John 7:27-28).
"Where I am, you can't come" is said to His enemies here, and later to His friends at the last supper - with a promise added for the friends that is not given to the enemies (John 7:34, 13:33, 14:3).
"The dispersion among the Greeks" means the Jews living scattered across the Greek-speaking world. They mean it as a sneer. John's readers knew the message did exactly that (John 7:35).

The last and greatest day of the feast is either the seventh day, when the water ceremony reached its height, or the eighth day, the solemn assembly Moses added to the end. Readers have argued both for a long time. The Torah gives the eighth day its own holy convocation (John 7:37, Leviticus 23:36).

Each morning of Tabernacles, a priest carried water from the pool of Siloam up to the temple and poured it out at the altar while the people sang. That ceremony is described in later Jewish writings rather than in the Torah, but it is the background that makes the shout land: on that day, at that feast, He offers water (John 7:37, Isaiah 12:3).
"He stood and cried out" - teachers normally sat. This was a man standing up in the temple court and shouting (John 7:37).

"As the Scripture has said" points to no single verse. The nearest are Zechariah 14, living waters going out from Jerusalem, and Ezekiel 47, water flowing from under the threshold of the temple - both prophecies associated with this very feast (John 7:38, Zechariah 14:8, Ezekiel 47:1).
"From within him" can be read two ways: out of the believer, or out of the Messiah Himself. John's next sentence, about the Spirit, suggests the source is Him and the channel is us (John 7:38-39).
"The Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn't yet glorified." John is writing from the far side of the cross, and he tells you so (John 7:39).
Some in the crowd object that the Christ comes from Bethlehem, of the seed of David. John reports it without comment - because every one of his readers knew where He was born (John 7:42, Micah 5:2).
"No man ever spoke like this man!" The officers were sent to arrest Him and came back arrested by what they heard (John 7:46).
"This multitude that doesn't know the law is cursed." The leaders' contempt for ordinary people is said out loud (John 7:49).

Nicodemus, who came by night in chapter 3, now speaks up in daylight, on a point of Torah: do we judge a man before hearing him? It is a small step, and it costs him (John 7:50-51, Deuteronomy 1:16-17).

"No prophet has arisen out of Galilee" is simply not true. Jonah was from Gath Hepher, a town in Galilee in the territory of Zebulun. In their anger the experts forgot their own Scriptures (John 7:52, 2 Kings 14:25).

The story of the woman taken in adultery, which follows, is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts of John and turns up in different places in later ones. Most readers believe it is a true story about Yahshua, preserved separately; the WEB prints it here (John 7:53).

intro: The chapter is set at Tabernacles, the most joyful week in the calendar: the harvest gathered, whole households living in booths, the branches waved, and Israel rejoicing before Yahweh in memory of the wilderness. It opens with His brothers mocking Him, urging Him to go and perform in public, because no one who wants to be known works in secret. John says plainly that even His brothers did not believe in Him - the boys raised in the same house - though one of them, James, would later lead the assembly in Jerusalem.

He tells them His time has not yet come, and that theirs is always ready, because nothing they do costs them anything. Then He goes up quietly and on His own terms. Jerusalem is murmuring about Him, divided between a good man and a deceiver, and no one speaks openly for fear. Halfway through the feast He begins teaching in the temple, and the experts ask how a man who never studied under a rabbi knows so much. His teaching, He says, belongs to the one who sent Him, and anyone willing to do God's will will know whether it is true - understanding following obedience rather than preceding it.

Then He turns the accusation around. Moses gave them the Torah and none of them keeps it, since they are plotting a murder while defending the Sabbath. They circumcise on the Sabbath because the eighth day takes precedence; why be angry that He made a whole man well? Judge not by appearance but with righteous judgment, He says, quoting the charge Deuteronomy gives every judge in Israel.

On the last and greatest day of the feast - in a week when, by later Jewish accounts, water was carried each morning from Siloam and poured out at the altar - He stands and cries out that anyone who thirsts should come to Him and drink, and that rivers of living water will flow from within. Zechariah's living waters from Jerusalem and Ezekiel's river from beneath the temple are both prophecies tied to this feast, and He claims them. John explains that He meant the Spirit, not yet given. The crowd divides over whether the Christ can come from Galilee, unaware of Bethlehem. The officers sent to arrest Him return saying no one ever spoke like this man. Nicodemus, who came by night, asks in daylight for a fair hearing, and is told that no prophet comes from Galilee - which forgets that Jonah came from Gath Hepher.

verses.1: After these things, Jesus was walking in Galilee, for he wouldn’t walk in Judea, because the Jews sought to kill him.
verses.2: Now the feast of the Jews, the Feast of Booths, was at hand.
verses.3: His brothers therefore said to him, “Depart from here, and go into Judea, that your disciples also may see your works which you do.
verses.4: For no one does anything in secret, and himself seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world.”
verses.5: For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.
verses.6: Jesus therefore said to them, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready.
verses.7: The world can’t hate you, but it hates me, because I testify about it, that its works are evil.
verses.8: You go up to the feast. I am not yet going up to this feast, because my time is not yet fulfilled.”
verses.9: Having said these things to them, he stayed in Galilee.
verses.10: But when his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly, but as it were in secret.
verses.11: The Jews therefore sought him at the feast, and said, “Where is he?”
verses.12: There was much murmuring among the multitudes concerning him. Some said, “He is a good man.” Others said, “Not so, but he leads the multitude astray.”
verses.13: Yet no one spoke openly of him for fear of the Jews.
verses.14: But when it was now the middle of the feast, Jesus went up into the temple and taught.
verses.15: The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How does this man know letters, having never been educated?”
verses.16: Jesus therefore answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.
verses.17: If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.
verses.18: He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.
verses.19: Didn’t Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law? Why do you seek to kill me?”
verses.20: The multitude answered, “You have a demon! Who seeks to kill you?”
verses.21: Jesus answered them, “I did one work, and you all marvel because of it.
verses.22: Moses has given you circumcision (not that it is of Moses, but of the fathers), and on the Sabbath you circumcise a boy.
verses.23: If a boy receives circumcision on the Sabbath, that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me, because I made a man completely healthy on the Sabbath?
verses.24: Don’t judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
verses.25: Therefore some of them of Jerusalem said, “Isn’t this he whom they seek to kill?
verses.26: Behold, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Can it be that the rulers indeed know that this is truly the Christ?
verses.27: However we know where this man comes from, but when the Christ comes, no one will know where he comes from.”
verses.28: Jesus therefore cried out in the temple, teaching and saying, “You both know me, and know where I am from. I have not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you don’t know.
verses.29: I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.”
verses.30: They sought therefore to take him; but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.
verses.31: But of the multitude, many believed in him. They said, “When the Christ comes, he won’t do more signs than those which this man has done, will he?”
verses.32: The Pharisees heard the multitude murmuring these things concerning him, and the chief priests and the Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.
verses.33: Then Jesus said, “I will be with you a little while longer, then I go to him who sent me.
verses.34: You will seek me, and won’t find me; and where I am, you can’t come.”
verses.35: The Jews therefore said among themselves, “Where will this man go that we won’t find him? Will he go to the Dispersion among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks?
verses.36: What is this word that he said, ‘You will seek me, and won’t find me; and where I am, you can’t come’?”
verses.37: Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!
verses.38: He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.”
verses.39: But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified.
verses.40: Many of the multitude therefore, when they heard these words, said, “This is truly the prophet.”
verses.41: Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “What, does the Christ come out of Galilee?
verses.42: Hasn’t the Scripture said that the Christ comes of the offspring of David, and from Bethlehem, the village where David was?”
verses.43: So there arose a division in the multitude because of him.
verses.44: Some of them would have arrested him, but no one laid hands on him.
verses.45: The officers therefore came to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to them, “Why didn’t you bring him?”
verses.46: The officers answered, “No man ever spoke like this man!”
verses.47: The Pharisees therefore answered them, “You aren’t also led astray, are you?
verses.48: Have any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees?
verses.49: But this multitude that doesn’t know the law is accursed.”
verses.50: Nicodemus (he who came to him by night, being one of them) said to them,
verses.51: “Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him personally and knows what he does?”
verses.52: They answered him, “Are you also from Galilee? Search, and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee.”
verses.53: Everyone went to his own house,

You shall rejoice in your feast, you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your gates.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 8 - Stones Dropped in the Temple Court, the Light of the World, and Before Abraham, I AM
chapters.title: Stones Dropped in the Temple Court, the Light of the World, and Before Abraham, I AM
keyNotes: He went to the Mount of Olives and came back to the temple at dawn. That is the pattern the other Gospels give for His final week, which is one reason many think this story belongs to that week (John 8:1-2, Luke 21:37-38).

The scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in the act. If she was caught in the act, the man was caught too. The Torah required both to die. They brought only one (John 8:3-4, Leviticus 20:10, Deuteronomy 22:22).
The trap was precise. Say no, and He contradicts Moses. Say yes, and He defies Rome, which reserved the death penalty for itself (John 8:5-6, 18:31).

He stooped and wrote on the ground with His finger. The tablets of the covenant were written with the finger of God. And Jeremiah says those who turn from Yahweh will be written in the earth (John 8:6, Exodus 31:18, Jeremiah 17:13).
What He wrote is never told. Every guess, including the popular one that He wrote their sins, is a guess (John 8:6, 8:8).

"He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her." Under the Torah the witnesses threw first. He did not abolish the penalty. He asked who was qualified to begin it (John 8:7, Deuteronomy 17:7).
They left one by one, beginning from the oldest. The older you are, the longer the list (John 8:9).
"Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more." Both halves matter, and in that order. He does not condemn her, and He does not call it nothing (John 8:11).

"I am the light of the world." At Tabernacles, according to later Jewish accounts, huge lamps were lit in the Court of the Women, bright enough to light the whole city. Verse 20 places Him in the treasury, which was in that same court (John 8:12, 8:20).

"Will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life" recalls the pillar of fire in the wilderness - the light Israel followed, which the feast of booths remembers (John 8:12, Exodus 13:21).

Their objection is a legal one: you testify about yourself, so your testimony is not valid. He answers with the Torah's own rule of two witnesses - Himself and the Father (John 8:13, 8:17-18, Deuteronomy 19:15).

"Unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins." The word he is not in the Greek. It reads: unless you believe that I am. Isaiah uses the same words for Yahweh: that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he (John 8:24, Isaiah 43:10).
"When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he." The cross will be the place where who He is becomes plain - lifted up, like the serpent on the pole (John 8:28, 3:14).

"You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free" is said to people who had just believed - and within twenty verses they are calling Him demon-possessed. Belief that will not stay is the subject of this whole exchange (John 8:31-32, 8:48).

"We have never been in bondage to anyone." Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, and the Roman soldiers standing outside the temple at that moment would beg to differ (John 8:33, Deuteronomy 6:21).
"Everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin." The slavery He means is not political (John 8:34).
"A bondservant doesn't live in the house forever. A son remains forever." Ishmael and Isaac. Sarah's words - cast out the servant and her son - stand behind the saying (John 8:35, Genesis 21:10).
"If you were Abraham's children, you would do the works of Abraham." Descent is not the same as likeness. Abraham welcomed messengers from God; they want to kill one (John 8:39-40).
"We were not born of sexual immorality" may be a jab. The rumors about His own birth were already going around (John 8:41).

"He was a murderer from the beginning" goes back to the garden and the lie that brought death, and to Cain, the first murderer, who John later says was of the evil one (John 8:44, Genesis 3:4, 1 John 3:12).
"Which of you convicts me of sin?" No one answers. In a crowd that wanted Him dead, no one could name a single thing (John 8:46).
"You are a Samaritan, and have a demon" - the two worst things they could think to call Him, in one breath (John 8:48).
"If a person keeps my word, he will never see death." They hear it as madness, because Abraham died and the prophets died (John 8:51-53).

"Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day." On the mountain, when Abraham said God will provide the lamb, and named the place Yahweh Will Provide, he was looking further than he knew (John 8:56, Genesis 22:8, 22:14).
"You are not yet fifty years old" is not a guess at His age. It is the age at which a Levite retired from service - a round number for a man not yet old (John 8:57, Numbers 4:3).
"Before Abraham came into existence, I AM." Not I was, which would claim age. I am, which claims something else. Abraham came to be; He simply is (John 8:58, Exodus 3:14).
They picked up stones. The Torah's penalty for blasphemy was stoning. They understood exactly what He had claimed (John 8:59, Leviticus 24:16).

"Jesus was hidden, and went out of the temple." In Ezekiel, the glory of Yahweh left the temple and went to the mountain on the east. John lets the picture stand without comment (John 8:59, Ezekiel 10:18, 11:23).

intro: At dawn in the temple court the scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in the act of adultery and stand her before the crowd. If she was caught in the act, the man was too, and the Torah condemned both; they brought only one, which shows this was never about the Torah. The trap was precise: refusing would set Him against Moses, and assenting would defy Rome, which kept the power of execution for itself. He stoops and writes on the ground with His finger - the finger that wrote the tablets at Sinai - in the dust where, Jeremiah said, those who turn from Yahweh are written. What He wrote is never told.

Pressed, He says that the one without sin should throw the first stone. In the Torah the witnesses threw first, so He has not abolished the penalty; He has asked who is qualified to begin it. They leave one by one, beginning with the oldest. Alone with her, He tells her that He does not condemn her, and that from now on she is to sin no more. Both halves stand, in that order.

Then, standing by the treasury in the Court of the Women, where by later Jewish accounts the great lamps of Tabernacles lit the whole city, He says that He is the light of the world. The exchange that follows hardens steadily. Unless they believe that I am, He says, using Isaiah's words for Yahweh, they will die in their sins. To those who had believed He promises that the truth will make them free, and they protest that Abraham's children have never been slaves to anyone - an astonishing claim from a people who had known Egypt and Babylon and stood at that moment under Rome. The slavery He means is to sin, and only the Son, who remains in the house, can set them free.

Descent from Abraham, He says, is not the same as likeness to him; their desire to kill Him shows a different father. He asks which of them can convict Him of sin, and no one answers. When He promises that whoever keeps His word will never see death, they invoke Abraham's death, and He replies that Abraham rejoiced to see His day. Then the sentence: before Abraham came into existence, I AM. Abraham had a beginning; He simply is. They pick up stones, the Torah's penalty for blasphemy, understanding Him perfectly, and He passes out of the temple, as the glory once left it in Ezekiel's vision.

verses.1: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.
verses.2: Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down, and taught them.
verses.3: The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery. Having set her in the middle,
verses.4: they told him, “Teacher, we found this woman in adultery, in the very act.
verses.5: Now in our law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. What then do you say about her?”
verses.6: They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of. But Jesus stooped down, and wrote on the ground with his finger.
verses.7: But when they continued asking him, he looked up and said to them, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.”
verses.8: Again he stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground.
verses.9: They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle.
verses.10: Jesus, standing up, saw her and said, “Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?”
verses.11: She said, “No one, Lord.” Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.”
verses.12: Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”
verses.13: The Pharisees therefore said to him, “You testify about yourself. Your testimony is not valid.”
verses.14: Jesus answered them, “Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from, and where I am going; but you don’t know where I came from, or where I am going.
verses.15: You judge according to the flesh. I judge no one.
verses.16: Even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for I am not alone, but I am with the Father who sent me.
verses.17: It’s also written in your law that the testimony of two people is valid.
verses.18: I am one who testifies about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me.”
verses.19: They said therefore to him, “Where is your Father?” Jesus answered, “You know neither me, nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.”
verses.20: Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, as he taught in the temple. Yet no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
verses.21: Jesus said therefore again to them, “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sins. Where I go, you can’t come.”
verses.22: The Jews therefore said, “Will he kill himself, because he says, ‘Where I am going, you can’t come’?”
verses.23: He said to them, “You are from beneath. I am from above. You are of this world. I am not of this world.
verses.24: I said therefore to you that you will die in your sins; for unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.”
verses.25: They said therefore to him, “Who are you?” Jesus said to them, “Just what I have been saying to you from the beginning.
verses.26: I have many things to speak and to judge concerning you. However he who sent me is true; and the things which I heard from him, these I say to the world.”
verses.27: They didn’t understand that he spoke to them about the Father.
verses.28: Jesus therefore said to them, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and I do nothing of myself, but as my Father taught me, I say these things.
verses.29: He who sent me is with me. The Father hasn’t left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.”
verses.30: As he spoke these things, many believed in him.
verses.31: Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples.
verses.32: You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.”
verses.33: They answered him, “We are Abraham’s offspring, and have never been in bondage to anyone. How do you say, ‘You will be made free’?”
verses.34: Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin.
verses.35: A bondservant doesn’t live in the house forever. A son remains forever.
verses.36: If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.
verses.37: I know that you are Abraham’s offspring, yet you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you.
verses.38: I say the things which I have seen with my Father; and you also do the things which you have seen with your father.”
verses.39: They answered him, “Our father is Abraham.” Jesus said to them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham.
verses.40: But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth, which I heard from God. Abraham didn’t do this.
verses.41: You do the works of your father.” They said to him, “We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father, God.”
verses.42: Therefore Jesus said to them, “If God were your father, you would love me, for I came out and have come from God. For I haven’t come of myself, but he sent me.
verses.43: Why don’t you understand my speech? Because you can’t hear my word.
verses.44: You are of your father, the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and doesn’t stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks on his own; for he is a liar, and the father of lies.
verses.45: But because I tell the truth, you don’t believe me.
verses.46: Which of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?
verses.47: He who is of God hears the words of God. For this cause you don’t hear, because you are not of God.”
verses.48: Then the Jews answered him, “Don’t we say well that you are a Samaritan, and have a demon?”
verses.49: Jesus answered, “I don’t have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.
verses.50: But I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges.
verses.51: Most certainly, I tell you, if a person keeps my word, he will never see death.”
verses.52: Then the Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets; and you say, ‘If a man keeps my word, he will never taste of death.’
verses.53: Are you greater than our father, Abraham, who died? The prophets died. Who do you make yourself out to be?”
verses.54: Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say that he is our God.
verses.55: You have not known him, but I know him. If I said, ‘I don’t know him,’ I would be like you, a liar. But I know him, and keep his word.
verses.56: Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day. He saw it, and was glad.”
verses.57: The Jews therefore said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?”
verses.58: Jesus said to them, “Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM.”
verses.59: Therefore they took up stones to throw at him, but Jesus was hidden, and went out of the temple, having gone through the middle of them, and so passed by.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 9 - A Man Born Blind, Mud and a Pool Called Sent, and the Ones Who Could Not See
chapters.title: A Man Born Blind, Mud and a Pool Called Sent, and the Ones Who Could Not See
keyNotes: He saw a man blind from birth. In this Gospel He keeps noticing people first. The man never asked for anything (John 9:1).

"Who sinned, this man or his parents?" Both options had defenders. The commandment speaks of iniquity visited on the children of those who hate Him; Ezekiel says the son will not bear the father's iniquity (John 9:2, Exodus 20:5, Ezekiel 18:20).
"Neither did this man sin, nor his parents." He rejects the whole question. Not every suffering is a sentence (John 9:3, 5:14).

"That the works of God might be revealed in him" can be punctuated differently, since the Greek had no punctuation: neither he nor his parents sinned. But so that the works of God may be revealed, we must work. Either way, the blindness is not a punishment (John 9:3-4).
"I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day." The WEB reads I; many of the oldest manuscripts read we must work, which takes the disciples into the work with Him (John 9:4).
He spat on the ground and made mud. God formed man from the dust of the ground. The one who made eyes the first time uses the same material the second time (John 9:6, Genesis 2:7).

Siloam means Sent. It was the pool at the bottom of the city, fed by the waters of Shiloah that Isaiah says the people refused - the same pool the water came from at the feast two chapters earlier (John 9:7, Isaiah 8:6).
He went, washed, and came back seeing. He had to walk to the pool blind, with mud on his face, on nothing but a word (John 9:7).
The neighbors cannot agree whether it is even the same man. Some say yes, some say it looks like him. A changed life is often harder for people to accept than a miracle (John 9:8-9).

"It was a Sabbath" - again held back until after the healing, as in chapter 5. Kneading clay was one of the forms of work later listed as forbidden on the Sabbath. The Torah's own command is to do no regular work and to keep the day holy (John 9:14, 5:9).
The Pharisees split: he is not from God because he does not keep the Sabbath; how can a sinner do such signs? The miracle forced a choice they did not want to make (John 9:16).
"He is a prophet" is the man's first answer. Watch him move: a man called Jesus, then a prophet, then from God, then Lord, then worship (John 9:11, 9:17, 9:33, 9:38).
His parents confirm the facts and refuse anything else: he is of age, ask him. They feared being put out of the synagogue, a word found only in John (John 9:20-22, 12:42, 16:2).
"Give glory to God" was a solemn charge to tell the truth and confess. Joshua said it to Achan before Achan admitted his sin (John 9:24, Joshua 7:19).
"One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see." He cannot answer their theology. He can answer from experience, and they have no reply to that (John 9:25).
"You don't also want to become his disciples, do you?" The word also means the blind beggar already counts himself one (John 9:27).
"We are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses." Moses saw God face to face, and Moses wrote about the one standing in front of them (John 9:28-29, Deuteronomy 34:10, 5:46).

"We know that God doesn't listen to sinners" is the man quoting their own theology back at them, and he is right. Yahweh is far from the wicked but hears the prayer of the righteous (John 9:31, Proverbs 15:29).

"Since the world began it has never been heard of that anyone opened the eyes of someone born blind." The Hebrew Scriptures record no such miracle. Psalm 146 says it is something Yahweh does (John 9:32, Psalm 146:8).
"You were altogether born in sins, and do you teach us?" They answer the logic with an insult and throw him out (John 9:34).
"Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and finding him..." Thrown out by men, found by Him. He went looking (John 9:35).
"Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?" The man has never seen Yahshua. He went to the pool blind and came back to find Him gone (John 9:36).
"You have both seen him, and it is he who speaks with you." The first face the man ever looked at with understanding was His (John 9:37).
"He worshiped him." The same word used for worship given to God. Yahshua does not stop him (John 9:38).

"I came into this world for judgment, that those who don't see may see, and that those who see may become blind" is Isaiah's commission running in both directions at once (John 9:39, Isaiah 6:9-10, 29:18).
"If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, 'We see.' Therefore your sin remains." The blindness that cannot be healed is the kind that insists it can see (John 9:41).

intro: Yahshua sees a man blind from birth who asks for nothing, and the disciples see a theological question: who sinned, this man or his parents? Both answers had Scripture behind them, the commandment's iniquity of the fathers on one side and Ezekiel's refusal to make the son bear the father's guilt on the other. He rejects the question entirely. Neither sinned; not every suffering is a sentence. Then He spits on the ground, makes mud, and anoints the man's eyes - the same material from which man was formed in Genesis - and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam, a name John translates as Sent. The man walks there blind with mud on his face, on nothing but a word, and comes back seeing.

What follows is close to comedy. The neighbors cannot agree that it is the same man. The Pharisees, told that the healing happened on a Sabbath, split between those who say a Sabbath-breaker cannot be from God and those who ask how a sinner could do such signs. The man's parents confirm that he is their son and was born blind, and refuse to say anything more, afraid of being put out of the synagogue. Recalled and charged to give glory to God, the formula Joshua used to bring Achan to confession, the man answers with the one thing no argument can touch: he was blind and now he sees.

When they demand the story again he asks whether they want to become His disciples too, counting himself one already. They retreat to Moses, to whom God spoke, and the beggar takes up their own theology and turns it on them: God does not hear sinners, no one since the world began has opened the eyes of a man born blind, and if this man were not from God He could do nothing. They answer with an insult and throw him out.

Then Yahshua, hearing it, goes and finds him. The man has never seen Him; he left for the pool blind and returned to find Him gone. Asked whether he believes in the Son of Man, he asks who He is, and is told he has seen Him and is speaking with Him now. He says, Lord, I believe, and worships Him. Across the chapter he has moved from a man called Jesus to a prophet, to one from God, to Lord, to worship. The chapter closes on the reversal: the blind made to see, and those who insist they see left in their sin.

verses.1: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth.
verses.2: His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
verses.3: Jesus answered, “Neither did this man sin, nor his parents; but, that the works of God might be revealed in him.

verses.5: While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”
verses.6: When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, anointed the blind man’s eyes with the mud,
verses.7: and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So he went away, washed, and came back seeing.
verses.8: The neighbors therefore, and those who saw that he was blind before, said, “Isn’t this he who sat and begged?”
verses.9: Others were saying, “It is he.” Still others were saying, “He looks like him.” He said, “I am he.”
verses.10: They therefore were asking him, “How were your eyes opened?”
verses.11: He answered, “A man called Jesus made mud, anointed my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go to the pool of Siloam, and wash.’ So I went away and washed, and I received sight.”
verses.12: Then they asked him, “Where is he?” He said, “I don’t know.”
verses.13: They brought him who had been blind to the Pharisees.
verses.14: It was a Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.
verses.15: Again therefore the Pharisees also asked him how he received his sight. He said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, I washed, and I see.”
verses.16: Some therefore of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, because he doesn’t keep the Sabbath.” Others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” There was division among them.
verses.17: Therefore they asked the blind man again, “What do you say about him, because he opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.”
verses.18: The Jews therefore did not believe concerning him, that he had been blind, and had received his sight, until they called the parents of him who had received his sight,
verses.19: and asked them, “Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”
verses.20: His parents answered them, “We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind;
verses.21: but how he now sees, we don’t know; or who opened his eyes, we don’t know. He is of age. Ask him. He will speak for himself.”
verses.22: His parents said these things because they feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed that if any man would confess him as Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue.
verses.23: Therefore his parents said, “He is of age. Ask him.”
verses.24: So they called the man who was blind a second time, and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.”
verses.25: He therefore answered, “I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.”
verses.26: They said to him again, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”
verses.27: He answered them, “I told you already, and you didn’t listen. Why do you want to hear it again? You don’t also want to become his disciples, do you?”
verses.28: They insulted him and said, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.
verses.29: We know that God has spoken to Moses. But as for this man, we don’t know where he comes from.”
verses.30: The man answered them, “How amazing! You don’t know where he comes from, yet he opened my eyes.
verses.31: We know that God doesn’t listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God, and does his will, he listens to him.
verses.32: Since the world began it has never been heard of that anyone opened the eyes of someone born blind.
verses.33: If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”
verses.34: They answered him, “You were altogether born in sins, and do you teach us?” They threw him out.
verses.35: Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and finding him, he said, “Do you believe in the Son of God?”
verses.36: He answered, “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?”
verses.37: Jesus said to him, “You have both seen him, and it is he who speaks with you.”
verses.38: He said, “Lord, I believe!” and he worshiped him.
verses.39: Jesus said, “I came into this world for judgment, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind.”
verses.40: Those of the Pharisees who were with him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?”
verses.41: Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see.’ Therefore your sin remains.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 10 - The Door, the Good Shepherd, and I and the Father Are One
chapters.title: The Door, the Good Shepherd, and I and the Father Are One
keyNotes: There is no break between chapters 9 and 10. The shepherds He is describing are the same men who just threw a healed sheep out of the fold (John 10:1, 9:34).
A sheepfold was a walled enclosure, often shared by several flocks overnight. A thief does not use the door because the doorkeeper knows who belongs and who does not (John 10:1-3).

"He calls his own sheep by name." Shepherds in the region still do this, and the sheep come. Yahweh told Moses I know you by name, and told Jacob I have called you by your name, you are mine (John 10:3, Exodus 33:17, Isaiah 43:1).
"He goes before them." An eastern shepherd leads from the front. The sheep follow a voice, not a stick (John 10:4).
John calls it a paroimia, a figure of speech, and says they did not understand it. So He tells it again from another angle (John 10:6).
"I am the door" is the third of the seven I AM sayings with a picture. A shepherd would sometimes sleep across the gap in the wall. He was literally the door (John 10:7, 10:9).

"Will go in and go out, and will find pasture" is covenant language for a life safely led. Moses asked for a man who would go out and come in before the people, so they would not be like sheep without a shepherd (John 10:9, Numbers 27:17).

"The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly." Abundantly means beyond what is needed, overflowing. He did not come to keep people barely alive (John 10:10, Psalm 36:8).
"Good shepherd" uses kalos, which means good in the sense of noble, beautiful, the real thing - as opposed to the worthless shepherds condemned by the prophets (John 10:11, Zechariah 11:17).

Ezekiel 34 is the background of the whole chapter. Yahweh condemns the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves, and then says: I myself will search for my sheep, I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep. And then: I will set up one shepherd over them, my servant David. Both are true of Yahshua at once (John 10:11, Ezekiel 34:2, 34:15, 34:23).
"Lays down his life for the sheep." A shepherd might risk his life for the flock. This one plans to give it, and says so five times in the chapter (John 10:11, 15, 17, 18).
The hired hand flees when the wolf comes because the sheep are not his. You find out who owns the flock when it costs something (John 10:12-13).
"I know my own, and I'm known by my own; even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father." The way He knows His sheep is compared to the way He and the Father know each other (John 10:14-15).

"Other sheep, which are not of this fold" is usually read of the nations coming in. Ezekiel 37 speaks of the two houses, Judah and Joseph, gathered back as one nation with one shepherd over them. Either way the destination is the same: one flock, one shepherd (John 10:16, Ezekiel 37:22-24).

"I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it away from me." The cross was not something that happened to Him. He had authority to lay it down and authority to take it up (John 10:17-18).

The Feast of Dedication remembers the cleansing and rededication of the temple after Antiochus Epiphanes defiled it, nearly two hundred years earlier. It is not one of the appointed times in Leviticus 23. John simply records that Yahshua was in the temple at that time, in winter (John 10:22-23).
Solomon's porch was a covered colonnade along the east side of the temple court, a place out of the winter weather. The early believers later met there (John 10:23, Acts 5:12).
"How long will you hold us in suspense?" is literally how long will you take away our life, or lift up our soul. They want a straight answer they can use (John 10:24).

"No one will snatch them out of my hand... no one is able to snatch them out of my Father's hand." The same hand, said two ways. Yahweh says in Isaiah: there is no one who can deliver out of my hand (John 10:28-29, Isaiah 43:13).
"I and the Father are one" uses one in the neuter, hen - one thing, not one person. It is the unity of the Shema, Yahweh is one, spoken from inside it (John 10:30, Deuteronomy 6:4).
They pick up stones because, as they say, you, being a man, make yourself God. Once again His enemies understood Him more clearly than many readers since (John 10:31-33).

"I said, you are gods" is Psalm 82, which Yahshua calls your law - the word could cover the whole of Scripture. In the psalm God stands among those He calls gods and sons of the Most High and says they will die like men. Readers divide over whether they are Israel's judges or the heavenly council; the argument works either way (John 10:34, Psalm 82:6-7).
The argument runs from lesser to greater. If Scripture can call them gods, how can you call it blasphemy when the one the Father set apart and sent says I am the Son of God? (John 10:35-36).
"The Scripture can't be broken" is said in passing, as something everyone in the conversation already agreed on (John 10:35).
"Sanctified and sent" - set apart and sent - is said at the feast of setting apart. Dedication remembered an altar consecrated again; He claims to be the one the Father consecrated (John 10:36).
He goes back across the Jordan to where John first baptized. The ministry ends near where it began (John 10:40, 1:28).
"John did no sign, but everything John said about this man is true." The best thing ever said about a preacher (John 10:41).

intro: Chapter 10 follows directly from the man thrown out of the synagogue, and Yahshua turns to the men who threw him out and speaks of shepherds. Every hearer knew the prophets' indictment: Ezekiel's shepherds who feed themselves instead of the flock, Jeremiah's who scatter the sheep of Yahweh's pasture. The thief climbs over the wall rather than using the door; the true shepherd calls his own sheep by name, as Yahweh knew Moses by name and called Jacob by his, goes before them, and is followed because they know his voice.

Then come two of the I AM sayings in succession. I am the door - the shepherd who lay across the opening of the stone fold at night, so that nothing passed except over him. The thief comes to steal and kill and destroy; He came that they might have life overflowing. And I am the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep. Ezekiel 34 holds the key: Yahweh condemns the false shepherds and says that He Himself will seek and shepherd His sheep, and then that He will set over them one shepherd, His servant David. Yahshua is both. The hired hand flees from the wolf because the sheep are not his, and there are other sheep, not of this fold, who will hear His voice until there is one flock and one shepherd - whether read of the nations, or of Ezekiel's two houses made one nation under one shepherd. No one takes His life from Him. He lays it down and takes it up again on His own authority.

At the Feast of Dedication, in winter, in Solomon's porch, He is surrounded and asked to say plainly whether He is the Christ. His sheep hear His voice, He says, and no one will snatch them from His hand or from His Father's hand - the same hand, spoken of twice - and then: I and the Father are one, the unity of the Shema spoken from within. They take up stones, saying that He, a man, makes Himself God. He answers from Psalm 82, where Scripture, which cannot be broken, calls others gods: how then is it blasphemy for the one the Father set apart and sent to say He is the Son of God? It is a striking word at the feast of setting apart. He withdraws beyond the Jordan, where John had baptized, and the people there remember that John did no sign, but everything he said about this man was true.

verses.1: “Most certainly, I tell you, one who doesn’t enter by the door into the sheep fold, but climbs up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.
verses.2: But one who enters in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.
verses.3: The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out.
verses.4: Whenever he brings out his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.
verses.5: They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him; for they don’t know the voice of strangers.”
verses.6: Jesus spoke this parable to them, but they didn’t understand what he was telling them.
verses.7: Jesus therefore said to them again, “Most certainly, I tell you, I am the sheep’s door.
verses.8: All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep didn’t listen to them.
verses.9: I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out, and will find pasture.
verses.10: The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.
verses.11: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
verses.12: He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who doesn’t own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The wolf snatches the sheep, and scatters them.
verses.13: The hired hand flees because he is a hired hand, and doesn’t care for the sheep.
verses.14: I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and I’m known by my own;
verses.15: even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father. I lay down my life for the sheep.
verses.16: I have other sheep, which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. They will become one flock with one shepherd.
verses.17: Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again.
verses.18: No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.”
verses.19: Therefore a division arose again among the Jews because of these words.
verses.20: Many of them said, “He has a demon, and is insane! Why do you listen to him?”
verses.21: Others said, “These are not the sayings of one possessed by a demon. It isn’t possible for a demon to open the eyes of the blind, is it?”
verses.22: It was the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem.
verses.23: It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s porch.
verses.24: The Jews therefore came around him and said to him, “How long will you hold us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”
verses.25: Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you don’t believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me.
verses.26: But you don’t believe, because you are not of my sheep, as I told you.
verses.27: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
verses.28: I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
verses.29: My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand.
verses.30: I and the Father are one.”
verses.31: Therefore Jews took up stones again to stone him.
verses.32: Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of those works do you stone me?”
verses.33: The Jews answered him, “We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy: because you, being a man, make yourself God.”
verses.34: Jesus answered them, “Isn’t it written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods?’
verses.35: If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came (and the Scripture can’t be broken),
verses.36: do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God?’
verses.37: If I don’t do the works of my Father, don’t believe me.
verses.38: But if I do them, though you don’t believe me, believe the works; that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in the Father.”
verses.39: They sought again to seize him, and he went out of their hand.
verses.40: He went away again beyond the Jordan into the place where John was baptizing at first, and there he stayed.
verses.41: Many came to him. They said, “John indeed did no sign, but everything that John said about this man is true.”

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 11 - Two Days' Delay, I Am the Resurrection, and Lazarus, Come Out
chapters.title: Two Days' Delay, I Am the Resurrection, and Lazarus, Come Out
keyNotes: Bethany was a village on the far side of the Mount of Olives, fifteen stadia - under two miles - from Jerusalem. Close enough to be dangerous (John 11:1, 11:18).
John identifies Mary as the one who anointed the Lord, though he does not tell that story until the next chapter. He assumes his readers already know it (John 11:2, 12:3).
"Lord, behold, he for whom you have great affection is sick." The sisters send no request. They send a description of the need and trust the love (John 11:3).
"This sickness is not to death" - and Lazarus dies. He means death will not be the end of it (John 11:4).

"Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. When therefore he heard that he was sick, he stayed two days." John puts the love and the delay side by side with the word therefore between them. The delay was not the opposite of the love (John 11:5-6).
The disciples remind Him that the Judeans just tried to stone Him. Going to Bethany means going back into range (John 11:8, 10:31).
"Aren't there twelve hours of daylight?" A man walking in the day does not stumble. His day had a set length, and nothing could cut it short (John 11:9-10).

"Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep." Scripture often calls death sleep, as Daniel speaks of those who sleep in the dust of the earth awakening. The disciples take Him literally, and He has to say it plainly: Lazarus is dead (John 11:11-14, Daniel 12:2).
"Let's go also, that we may die with him." Thomas, remembered for doubting, is the one who says this. Courage and doubt can live in the same man (John 11:16).

Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. There was a popular belief that the soul lingered near the body for three days. On the fourth day nobody could pretend he was not really dead (John 11:17, 11:39).
Many had come from Jerusalem to console the sisters. Mourning was public and lasted days, which means the miracle that follows will have a large audience (John 11:19, 11:45).
Martha goes out to meet Him; Mary sits in the house. The same two women as in Luke, behaving exactly as they did there (John 11:20, Luke 10:39-40).

"I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day." Martha's theology is correct, and it is the theology of Daniel 12. She believed in a resurrection someday. He is about to show her that someday is standing in front of her (John 11:24).
"I am the resurrection and the life" is the fifth of the seven I AM sayings with a picture. He does not say I will bring the resurrection. He says I am it (John 11:25).
"Do you believe this?" Martha's answer - You are the Christ, the Son of God, he who comes into the world - is almost word for word the purpose statement of the whole Gospel (John 11:27, 20:31).

Mary says exactly what Martha said: Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn't have died. To Martha He gave theology. To Mary He gives tears. Same sentence, different need (John 11:21, 11:32).
"He groaned in the spirit, and was troubled." The word for groaned can describe a horse snorting, and in Greek it carries anger. He was not only sad. He was angry at death itself (John 11:33, 11:38).

"Jesus wept" is the shortest verse in the English Bible. The word is different from the loud wailing of the mourners around Him. These were quiet tears, from a man who knew He was about to fix it (John 11:35).

"Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days." Martha, who said she believed, still tries to stop Him at the stone. Believing in theory and believing at the tomb are different things (John 11:39).
He prays out loud, and says why: for the sake of the crowd, that they may believe the Father sent Him. He thanks the Father before anything has happened (John 11:41-42).

"Lazarus, come out!" He calls him by name. Some have said that if He had not named him, every grave in the place would have emptied. It is a preview of the hour when all who are in the tombs will hear His voice (John 11:43, 5:28).
Lazarus comes out still bound, hands and feet, his face wrapped. Yahshua gives life; the people standing there are told to unwrap him. Loose him, and let him go (John 11:44).
Lazarus would die again. This is a raising, not yet the resurrection. The grave clothes stay behind in the tomb only when Yahshua Himself rises (John 11:44, 20:6-7).

The council meets because the miracle is too big to ignore. Their fear is that the Romans will take away both our place and our nation. The place means the temple. Forty years later the Romans did exactly that (John 11:47-48, Jeremiah 7:14).

Caiaphas was high priest that year, and says one man should die for the people rather than the whole nation perish. He meant it as cold politics. John says he was prophesying, because of his office, and did not know it (John 11:49-51).

"Not for the nation only, but that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad." The language of gathering the scattered is the prophets' language for the regathering of Israel, and of the nations with them (John 11:52, Ezekiel 37:21, Isaiah 11:12).
From that day they plotted to kill Him. Raising a dead man is what finally got Him killed (John 11:53).
He withdrew to a town called Ephraim, near the wilderness. It is the only time John mentions it (John 11:54).

Many went up to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves, since anyone unclean could not eat it. The Torah made provision for those who could not keep it at the first time (John 11:55, Numbers 9:10).

intro: Two sisters in Bethany send Yahshua a message that asks for nothing and simply names the need: the one you love is sick. Then John sets two sentences side by side: Yahshua loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus, and therefore, hearing of the sickness, He stayed where He was two more days. The delay is joined to the love by a therefore, not opposed to it. When He resolves to return to Judea, where He was nearly stoned, it is Thomas - remembered for doubting - who says let us go and die with Him. He speaks of Lazarus as asleep, in Scripture's familiar idiom for death, and then plainly: Lazarus is dead.

Lazarus has been four days in the tomb when they arrive, past any pretence that he was not truly dead. Martha meets Him on the road with a reproach - if you had been here - and a faith that God will give Him whatever He asks. Told her brother will rise, she answers with the correct theology of Daniel 12, the resurrection at the last day. He answers that He is the resurrection and the life, and her confession - the Christ, the Son of God, who comes into the world - nearly repeats the purpose of the whole Gospel. Mary comes and says exactly what her sister said, and receives no theology at all. He is deeply moved, with a word that carries anger at death itself, and He weeps, quietly, though He knows what He is about to do.

At the tomb Martha, who had confessed her faith on the road, tries to stop Him at the stone: four days, and the stench. The stone is moved; He thanks the Father aloud before anything happens, for the sake of the crowd, and calls Lazarus out by name with a loud voice - a preview of the hour when all in the tombs will hear Him. Lazarus comes out still bound, and the bystanders are told to loose him and let him go. He gives the life; others remove the grave clothes.

The miracle that should have ended the argument is the one that sets His death in motion. The council fears the Romans will take away their place, the temple, and their nation, and Caiaphas, high priest that year, counsels that one man should die for the people. He means it as cold policy; John says he was prophesying by virtue of his office, and that the death would gather into one the scattered children of God - the prophets' own language for regathering. From that day they plot to kill Him. He gave Lazarus his life, and it cost Him His.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 12 - A Pound of Nard, a King on a Donkey's Colt, and Isaiah Saw His Glory
chapters.title: A Pound of Nard, a King on a Donkey's Colt, and Isaiah Saw His Glory
keyNotes: "Six days before the Passover" begins the final week. From here, John slows down; the last third of his Gospel covers only a few days (John 12:1).
Martha served, Lazarus reclined at the table, and Mary poured. Three people, three ways of loving Him, none of them wrong (John 12:2-3).

A pound, litra, was about eleven ounces of pure nard - a perfume made from a plant that grew in the Himalayas. Judas priced it at three hundred denarii, about a year's wages for a laborer (John 12:3, 12:5).
Mark and Matthew say she poured it on His head. John says His feet. A pound of perfume is enough for both. Kings were anointed on the head; feet were the place a servant knelt (John 12:3, Mark 14:3).
She wiped His feet with her hair. A respectable woman did not let her hair down in front of men. She did not care what it cost her (John 12:3).

"The house was filled with the fragrance." The Song of Songs: while the king sat at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance. Everyone who left that house smelled of it (John 12:3, Song of Solomon 1:12).

Judas objects on behalf of the poor. John tells us he did not care about the poor; he kept the money box and stole from it. The loudest objection to extravagant worship came from the thief (John 12:4-6).
"She has kept this for the day of my burial." She may have understood what the twelve kept refusing to hear (John 12:7).

"You always have the poor with you" is Deuteronomy 15, which goes on: therefore open your hand wide to the poor. It is not permission to ignore them. It is a reminder that the chance to anoint Him was almost over (John 12:8, Deuteronomy 15:11).
The chief priests plot to kill Lazarus too, because he is evidence. A living man who had been dead four days was very bad for their case (John 12:10-11).

Palm branches are the branches of Tabernacles, commanded in Leviticus 23 for rejoicing before Yahweh, and they had become a symbol of national victory. The crowd is waving a feast and a liberation at the same time (John 12:13, Leviticus 23:40).
"Hosanna" is Hebrew for save now, from Psalm 118, one of the psalms sung at the feasts. Blessed is he who comes in the name of Yahweh is the next verse (John 12:13, Psalm 118:25-26).
"The King of Israel" is what Nathanael called Him in chapter 1. Now a whole city says it - and in a few days a sign over His head will say it in three languages (John 12:13, 1:49, 19:19).

He rides a young donkey, as Zechariah said - lowly, not on a warhorse. John opens the quotation with don't be afraid, daughter of Zion, words that echo Zephaniah (John 12:14-15, Zechariah 9:9, Zephaniah 3:16).
"His disciples didn't understand these things at first." John admits they missed it, and only connected the Scripture to the event after He was glorified (John 12:16).
"Look, the world has gone after him." They meant everyone. Two verses later the world arrives, in the form of Greeks (John 12:19-20).

The Greeks come to Philip, who has a Greek name and was from Bethsaida in Galilee. Philip goes to Andrew, and the two of them go to Yahshua. The same two men who brought people to Him in chapter 1 (John 12:21-22, 1:43-45).
"The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified." The hour that was not yet at Cana has arrived. And glorified, in this Gospel, means the cross (John 12:23, 2:4).

A grain of wheat that falls into the ground and dies bears much fruit. The day after the Sabbath during Unleavened Bread, the first sheaf of the harvest was waved before Yahweh - the firstfruits of what had been buried and come up (John 12:24, Leviticus 23:10-11).

"He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it." Hate is the Hebrew way of saying love less by comparison. It is about which life you are holding onto (John 12:25).
"Now my soul is troubled." This is John's Gethsemane. He asks out loud whether to pray to be saved from this hour, and answers Himself: no, for this cause I came to this hour (John 12:27).
A voice from heaven answers. Some heard thunder. Some said an angel spoke. The same sound, heard three ways, depending on the hearer (John 12:28-29).
"Now the prince of this world will be cast out." The cross looked like the defeat of Yahshua. It was the defeat of the one who held the world (John 12:31, Luke 10:18).

"If I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." Lifted up is the word from chapter 3 and chapter 8, and John explains it means the kind of death He would die (John 12:32-33, 3:14, 8:28).
"We have heard out of the law that the Christ remains forever." They are right - the throne of David's son is forever. What they cannot fit is a Christ who dies first (John 12:34, Psalm 89:36).

Isaiah 53:1 - who has believed our report - opens the suffering servant passage, and John quotes it over the end of the public ministry. The signs were done, and they still did not believe (John 12:37-38, Isaiah 53:1).

"Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him." The glory Isaiah saw was the Lord on the throne, high and lifted up, with the seraphim crying holy, holy, holy, Yahweh of Armies. John says that was Yahshua (John 12:41, Isaiah 6:1-3).

"High and lifted up" in Isaiah 6 is the same pair of words Isaiah uses for the suffering servant in chapter 52: exalted and lifted up, and very high. The throne and the cross are described in the same language (John 12:41, Isaiah 6:1, 52:13).

Many of the rulers believed in Him but would not confess it, for fear of being put out of the synagogue. They loved the praise of men more than the praise of God. Belief that will not be seen is a kind of fear (John 12:42-43).
"He who believes in me, believes not in me, but in him who sent me." To see Him is to see the Father (John 12:44-45, 14:9).

"The word that I spoke, the same will judge him in the last day." The promise of Deuteronomy 18: whoever will not listen to my words, which the prophet speaks in my name, I will require it of him (John 12:48, Deuteronomy 18:19).
"I know that his commandment is eternal life." The public ministry ends on the Father's commandment, and calls it life (John 12:50).

intro: Six days before Passover the final week begins at a dinner in Bethany. Martha serves, Lazarus - who had been dead - reclines at the table, and Mary pours a pound of pure nard, worth about a year's wages, over Yahshua's feet and wipes them with her hair, which a respectable woman did not let down in front of men. She counts neither the money nor her reputation, and the house is filled with the fragrance. Judas objects in the name of the poor, and John records that he was a thief who stole from the common purse. The loudest objection to extravagant worship comes from him. Yahshua defends her: she has kept it for His burial. She may have been the only one listening when He spoke of His death.

The next day a crowd goes out with palm branches - the branches of Tabernacles, taken in Leviticus to rejoice before Yahweh - crying Hosanna, save now, and blessed is he who comes in the name of Yahweh, from Psalm 118. He enters on a young donkey, lowly, as Zechariah foretold, and John admits that the disciples understood none of it until after He was glorified. Then Greeks come asking to see Jesus, and He answers that the hour has come - the hour that had not yet come at Cana - and speaks of a grain of wheat that must fall into the ground and die to bear fruit, the shape of the firstfruits sheaf waved before Yahweh during Unleavened Bread.

Here John shows his Gethsemane. His soul is troubled; shall He pray to be saved from this hour? No, for this He came. A voice answers from heaven, heard by some as thunder and by others as an angel. Now the prince of this world is cast out, and He, lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to Himself - lifted up, John explains, describing the death He would die.

John closes the public ministry with Isaiah: who has believed our report, and the eyes that were blinded. Then he adds that Isaiah said these things because he saw His glory. The glory Isaiah saw was the Lord enthroned, high and lifted up, with the seraphim crying holy to Yahweh of Armies - and John identifies Him as Yahshua. Isaiah uses the same words, high and lifted up, for the suffering servant whose face would be marred beyond any man's. The throne and the cross are spoken of in the same language. The chapter ends with rulers who believed but would not confess it, loving the praise of men more than the praise of God.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 13 - A Towel and a Basin, a Morsel Handed to a Traitor, and a New Commandment
chapters.title: A Towel and a Basin, a Morsel Handed to a Traitor, and a New Commandment
keyNotes: "Before the feast of the Passover" is John's own time stamp on this meal. The next morning the leaders will not enter the governor's house so that they can still eat the Passover, and the day of the crucifixion is called the preparation of the Passover. In John, this supper comes before the Passover meal (John 13:1, 18:28, 19:14).
"He loved them to the end" can also mean to the uttermost, completely. The word is from the same root as His last word on the cross: it is finished (John 13:1, 19:30).
Judas had already been given the thought by the devil before the washing began. Yahshua washed his feet knowing it (John 13:2, 13:11).
"Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands" - and what He did with all things in His hands was pick up a towel. Power, in this Gospel, kneels (John 13:3-4).

"Laid aside his outer garments" uses the same verb He used for laying down His life in chapter 10, and "put his outer garment back on" uses the same verb as taking it up again. The foot washing is the cross acted out in a room (John 13:4, 13:12, 10:17-18).

Washing feet was so low a task that it was given to the lowest servant in a house. Abigail offered to wash the feet of David's servants as the humblest thing she could say (John 13:5, 1 Samuel 25:41).
"You will never wash my feet!" Peter's refusal sounds humble and is actually pride. He wants to be the one who serves, not the one who needs it (John 13:8).
"If I don't wash you, you have no part with me." Being served by Him is not optional. Everyone who belongs to Him has to let Him kneel (John 13:8).

"Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed." A guest bathed at home and only his feet got dirty on the road. Cleansing once, and then daily washing of what the walk picks up (John 13:10, Exodus 30:19-21).
"You ought also to wash one another's feet." Some assemblies practice it literally; all are commanded the thing it means (John 13:14-15).
"A servant is not greater than his lord." Said here about serving, and repeated two chapters later about suffering (John 13:16, 15:20).
"He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me" is Psalm 41, David on a trusted friend who turned. To lift the heel is to kick, or to show contempt (John 13:18, Psalm 41:9).

"That you may believe that I am he" is ego eimi again, and again in the words of Isaiah: I declare the end from the beginning. He tells them beforehand so that the betrayal will confirm Him rather than shake them (John 13:19, Isaiah 46:10).
"He was troubled in spirit" - the same word used at Lazarus's tomb and in 12:27. Betrayal by a friend hurt Him (John 13:21, 11:33, 12:27).

They reclined at table, on their left sides, heads toward the table. The disciple whom Jesus loved was next to Him, at His breast - the same word used of the Son in the bosom of the Father (John 13:23, 1:18).

"The disciple whom Jesus loved" first appears here and is never named. The traditional answer is John the son of Zebedee, the author. He calls himself by the one thing he was sure of (John 13:23, 21:20-24).
To dip a piece of bread and hand it to someone was a mark of honor from the host. Boaz did it for Ruth. The last thing Yahshua offered Judas was friendship (John 13:26, Ruth 2:14).
"After the piece of bread, then Satan entered into him." He took the honor and left with the enemy (John 13:27).
"What you do, do quickly." No one at the table understood it. Some thought He was sending Judas to give something to the poor (John 13:27-29).
"He went out immediately. It was night." Four words in Greek. He walked away from the light of the world into the dark (John 13:30, 8:12).
"Now the Son of Man has been glorified." The moment the betrayer leaves, Yahshua calls it glory. The cross has begun (John 13:31).
"Little children" is the only time He calls them that in the Gospels. John picked it up and used it all through his letters (John 13:33, 1 John 2:1).
Love your neighbor as yourself was not new. It is in Leviticus 19. What is new is the measure: just as I have loved you. The standard moved from self to Him (John 13:34, Leviticus 19:18).
"By this everyone will know that you are my disciples." Not by doctrine, not by dress, not by argument - though all have their place. By love for one another (John 13:35).
"I will lay down my life for you." Peter means it, and he will draw a sword in the garden to prove it. Pride goes before a fall, and the fall is a few hours away (John 13:37, 18:10, Proverbs 16:18).
"The rooster won't crow until you have denied me three times." He predicts the failure, and in chapter 21 He will restore it three times over (John 13:38, 21:15-17).

intro: John dates the meal precisely: before the feast of the Passover. And he opens it with a sentence that governs the rest of the book - having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the end, to the uttermost, with a word from the same root as the cry it is finished. Knowing that the Father had given all things into His hands, Yahshua rises from supper, lays aside His outer garments, wraps a towel around His waist and washes the disciples' feet, the work of the lowest servant in a house. The verbs are the ones He used for laying down His life and taking it up again. The washing is the cross acted out in a room.

Peter refuses, which sounds like humility and is pride: he would rather serve than be served. Told that unless he is washed he has no part with Him, he asks for his head and hands as well, and is told that one who has bathed needs only his feet washed - a cleansing once, and then the daily washing of what the road picks up. Yahshua adds that not all of them are clean, because He knows who will betray Him, and He has washed that man's feet too. Then He tells them to do for one another what He has done for them.

Troubled in spirit, He announces that one of them will betray Him. Prompted by Peter, the disciple whom Jesus loved, reclining against His breast, asks who it is, and Yahshua answers by dipping a piece of bread and giving it to Judas - a host's gesture of honor. The last thing He offered Judas was friendship. After the bread Satan enters him, and he goes out. It was night. He walks away from the light of the world into the dark, and the moment he is gone Yahshua says that the Son of Man is glorified.

To the eleven, whom He calls little children for the only time, He gives a new commandment: love one another as I have loved you. Love of neighbor was as old as Leviticus 19; what is new is the measure, moved from self to Him, and He has just shown them what it looks like. Peter vows to lay down his life, and is told that before the rooster crows he will deny Him three times. At that table sat a betrayer and a man who would fail by morning, and He loved them to the end.

verses.6: Then he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”
verses.7: Jesus answered him, “You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later.”

verses.11: For he knew him who would betray him, therefore he said, “You are not all clean.”
verses.12: So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
verses.13: You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
verses.14: If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
verses.15: For I have given you an example, that you also should do as I have done to you.
verses.16: Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither one who is sent greater than he who sent him.
verses.17: If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.
verses.18: I don’t speak concerning all of you. I know whom I have chosen. But that the Scripture may be fulfilled, ‘He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me.’

verses.26: Jesus therefore answered, “It is he to whom I will give this piece of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the piece of bread, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
verses.27: After the piece of bread, then Satan entered into him. Then Jesus said to him, “What you do, do quickly.”
verses.28: Now no man at the table knew why he said this to him.
verses.29: For some thought, because Judas had the money box, that Jesus said to him, “Buy what things we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.

verses.32: If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and he will glorify him immediately.

verses.35: By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

verses.37: Peter said to him, “Lord, why can’t I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”
