chapters.heading: CHAPTER 14 - Let Not Your Heart Be Troubled, the Way to the Father, and Another Counselor
chapters.title: Let Not Your Heart Be Troubled, the Way to the Father, and Another Counselor
keyNotes: There is no chapter break in the conversation. Peter has just been told he will deny Him, and the next words are let not your heart be troubled. The comfort is spoken to a man about to fail (John 14:1, 13:38).
"You believe in God. Believe also in me." The Greek can be read as statements or commands. Either way He puts faith in Himself on the same level as faith in God (John 14:1).

"In my Father's house are many homes." The word for homes is related to the verb remain, which runs through these chapters. Dwelling places, places to stay. It reappears in verse 23 for the home the Father and Son make with the believer (John 14:2, 14:23).

"My Father's house" was the temple in chapter 2. Here it is bigger than any building. And Revelation ends with God's dwelling coming down to be with people, the holy city prepared like a bride (John 14:2, 2:16, Revelation 21:2-3).

Many readers hear a wedding in these verses: a bridegroom going ahead to prepare a place and coming back for his bride. The details often attached to it come from later sources, but the picture fits a Gospel that has already called Him the bridegroom (John 14:2-3, 3:29).
"I will come again, and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also." The promise is not first a place. It is a Person. Where I am (John 14:3).
"How can we know the way?" Thomas asks the honest question everyone else was too embarrassed to ask, and gets the answer the whole world quotes (John 14:5).
"I am the way, the truth, and the life" is the sixth of the seven I AM sayings with a picture. The earliest believers were called simply the Way (John 14:6, Acts 9:2).
"No one comes to the Father, except through me" is not a door slammed. It is a door opened, in the only place a door could be (John 14:6, 10:9).
"Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us." Moses asked: show me your glory, and was told no man may see my face and live (John 14:8, Exodus 33:18-20).
"He who has seen me has seen the Father." Philip had been looking at the answer to Moses's prayer for three years (John 14:9).
"I am in the Father, and the Father in me." Not two who agree. One who dwells in the other (John 14:10-11, 10:38).
"Greater works than these he will do" - greater in reach, not in kind. A few thousand heard Him in Galilee; the Way went to the ends of the earth (John 14:12).
"If you will ask anything in my name, I will do it." In His name means as His representative, on His business, the way an agent signs for the one who sent him (John 14:13-14).

"If you love me, keep my commandments" is the language of the ten commandments themselves: loving kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments. Love and obedience were never opposites (John 14:15, Exodus 20:6, Deuteronomy 7:9).
"Another Counselor" - parakletos, one called alongside, an advocate, a helper. And another means another of the same kind. The Spirit will be to them what He has been (John 14:16).
"He lives with you, and will be in you." Ezekiel promised it: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes (John 14:17, Ezekiel 36:27).
"I will not leave you orphans." A teacher's disciples were sometimes called his children, and a rabbi's death left them orphaned. He promises they will not be (John 14:18).
"Because I live, you will live also." His resurrection is the guarantee of theirs (John 14:19).
"He who has my commandments, and keeps them, that person is one who loves me." Said twice in seven verses, in case they missed it (John 14:15, 14:21).
Judas - not Iscariot - asks the only question this disciple asks in the Gospels: why show yourself to us and not to the world? (John 14:22).
"We will come to him, and make our home with him." I will set my tent among you, and walk among you, Yahweh said in Leviticus. The Father and the Son move in (John 14:23, Leviticus 26:11-12).
"He will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you." This is how the Gospel John is writing came to be remembered (John 14:26).

"Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you." Shalom was the ordinary goodbye. He gives it as an inheritance. Not as the world gives - the world gives peace by taking away the trouble; He gives it in the middle of it (John 14:27).
"The Father is greater than I" is said by the Son who has taken the form of a servant, going to the cross. It is the same Son who said I and the Father are one (John 14:28, 10:30).
"The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me." No foothold, no claim, nothing to hold onto (John 14:30).
"Arise, let us go from here." And then three more chapters of teaching. Many think they left the room here and the rest was spoken on the way to the garden (John 14:31, 18:1).

intro: The chapter follows directly on the prediction of Peter's denial, and its first words are let not your heart be troubled. The comfort is spoken to a man about to fail, before the failure rather than after it. Believe in God, He says, and believe also in Me, putting faith in Himself on the level of faith in God. In His Father's house - the temple of chapter 2, now enlarged beyond any building, and in Revelation the dwelling of God that comes down to be with people - are many dwelling places, and He goes to prepare one and will come again, so that where He is they may be. The promise is first a Person, then a place.

Thomas asks how they can know the way, and is told that Yahshua is the way, the truth and the life, and that no one comes to the Father except through Him - not a door closed but the only door that could be opened. Philip asks to be shown the Father, which is what Moses asked on the mountain and was refused, and he is told that whoever has seen Yahshua has seen the Father. He had been looking at the answer to Moses's prayer for three years.

If you love Me, keep My commandments: it is the language of the ten commandments themselves and of Deuteronomy's faithful God who keeps covenant with those who love Him and keep His commandments. Love and obedience were never opposed. With that comes the promise of another Counselor, an advocate called alongside, of the same kind as Yahshua Himself - the Spirit of truth, now with them and soon in them, as Ezekiel foresaw the Spirit placed within to cause Israel to walk in Yahweh's statutes.

They will not be left orphans. The Father and the Son will come and make their home with whoever keeps His word, using the word for the dwelling places of verse 2. The Spirit will teach them and remind them of everything He said, which is how this Gospel came to be remembered. Then He leaves them His peace, not as the world gives it by removing trouble, but in the middle of it - spoken to frightened men on the worst night of their lives. And He says: arise, let us go from here.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 15 - The True Vine, Greater Love, and Hated Without a Cause
chapters.title: The True Vine, Greater Love, and Hated Without a Cause
keyNotes: Israel was Yahweh's vine. You brought a vine out of Egypt, the psalm says. Isaiah sang about a vineyard that produced wild grapes. Jeremiah called Israel a noble vine turned degenerate (John 15:1, Psalm 80:8, Isaiah 5:1-2, Jeremiah 2:21).

"I am the true vine" is the last of the seven I AM sayings with a picture. Where Israel the vine failed to bear fruit, He is the vine that does. True means the real one that the others pointed to (John 15:1).
A great golden vine decorated the entrance to the temple, according to the historian Josephus. If they passed the temple on the way to the garden, it was in front of them (John 15:1, 14:31).
"My Father is the farmer." The vinedresser, the one who tends the vine. The whole operation is in the Father's hands (John 15:1).

"Every branch in me that doesn't bear fruit, he takes away." The verb can also mean lifts up, as vinedressers lift trailing branches off the ground so they can bear. The WEB reads takes away (John 15:2).

"Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes." Pruning is cutting, and it is done to the fruitful branches, not the dead ones. If you are being cut back, it may be because you are bearing (John 15:2, Isaiah 18:5).
"You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you." The same word in Greek serves for pruned and cleansed. The word He spoke was doing the cutting (John 15:3, 13:10).
"Remain in me" - the word remain, or abide, appears about ten times in the first ten verses. It is the single instruction of the chapter (John 15:4-10).
"Apart from me you can do nothing." Not less. Nothing (John 15:5).
A branch that does not remain is thrown out and burned. Ezekiel asked what vine wood is good for, and answered: not even a peg to hang a pot on - it is fuel (John 15:6, Ezekiel 15:2-4).
"If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire." His words remaining in us shape what we desire before we ask (John 15:7).

"In this is my Father glorified, that you bear much fruit." Fruit, in Scripture, is what a life produces - character and works both. Isaiah promised Israel would fill the world with fruit (John 15:8, Isaiah 27:6).

"If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love; even as I have kept my Father's commandments." The Son Himself kept the Father's commandments, and He holds that up as the pattern (John 15:10).
"That my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full." The whole chapter on pruning and remaining is aimed at joy (John 15:11, Psalm 16:11).
"Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." Said the night before He did exactly that (John 15:13).
"You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you." Friendship with Him is not casual. It shows in obedience (John 15:14).

"No longer do I call you servants... but I have called you friends." Abraham was called the friend of God. Yahweh spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. That privilege now extends to eleven ordinary men (John 15:15, Isaiah 41:8, Exodus 33:11).
A servant does not know what his master is doing. A friend is told. Everything He heard from the Father, He told them (John 15:15).

"You didn't choose me, but I chose you." Disciples normally chose their rabbi. He reverses it. Yahweh chose Israel, not because they were many but because He loved them (John 15:16, Deuteronomy 7:6-7).
"If the world hates you, you know that it has hated me before it hated you." Rejection of His people is not new information. It is His own experience extended (John 15:18).
"If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you." The prophets were seized and stoned in the temple courts for speaking Yahweh's word. The pattern is old (John 15:20, 2 Chronicles 24:21).
"They hated me without a cause" is written in their law, He says - meaning the Psalms, where David says it twice. The word law here covers all of Scripture (John 15:25, Psalm 35:19, 69:4).
"The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, will testify about me. You will also testify." Two witnesses again - the Spirit and the disciples (John 15:26-27, Deuteronomy 19:15).

intro: On the way from the upper room, Yahshua says that He is the true vine and His Father the farmer. Every hearer knew the vine was Israel: the vine brought out of Egypt in Psalm 80, the vineyard of Isaiah 5 that yielded wild grapes, the noble vine of Jeremiah 2 turned degenerate. Israel was the vine that kept failing to bear fruit, and He is the true vine, the one that does what the vine was planted to do.

The farmer removes branches that bear nothing and prunes those that bear, so that they bear more. The cutting falls on the fruitful branches, not the dead ones, and the disciples are already clean - the same word as pruned - through the word He has spoken to them. Then comes the single instruction of the chapter, repeated about ten times in ten verses: remain in Me. A branch bears nothing by itself; apart from Him they can do nothing at all, and a branch that does not remain withers and is burned, since vine wood, as Ezekiel observed, is good for nothing else.

Remaining is tied to obedience: keeping His commandments as He kept His Father's. And the aim of all of it, pruning and remaining and commandments alike, is that His joy may be in them and their joy full. Greater love, He says on the night before He shows it, has no one than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends. He no longer calls them servants, who do not know their master's business, but friends - the title of Abraham, the intimacy of Moses face to face - and He reminds them that they did not choose Him; He chose them, as Yahweh chose Israel, not for their numbers but for love.

Then He prepares them for what is coming. The world hated Him first and will hate them; if it persecuted Him it will persecute them, as it did the prophets before. It hated Him without a cause, as David wrote. And the Spirit of truth, proceeding from the Father, will testify about Him, and so will they - two witnesses, as the Torah requires.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 16 - It Is Good That I Go, a Woman in Labor, and I Have Overcome the World
chapters.title: It Is Good That I Go, a Woman in Labor, and I Have Overcome the World
keyNotes: "These things I have spoken to you, so that you wouldn't be caused to stumble." He warns them in advance so that the persecution confirms Him instead of shaking them (John 16:1, 16:4).
"Whoever kills you will think that he offers service to God." Saul of Tarsus did exactly that, and later said he thought it his duty (John 16:2, Acts 26:9-10).
"None of you asks me, 'Where are you going?'" Peter had asked earlier that night. Now grief has filled them so completely that they have stopped asking (John 16:5-6, 13:36).

"It is to your advantage that I go away." Better for them that He leave. While He was in a body He was in one place at a time; the Spirit would be with every one of them, everywhere (John 16:7, 14:16-17).
The Spirit will convict the world - expose it, prove it wrong - about three things: sin, righteousness, and judgment. Each gets a reason (John 16:8-11).
Sin, because they do not believe in Me. The root sin named here is not a list of actions but unbelief toward Him (John 16:9).
Righteousness, because I am going to the Father. The cross looked like the verdict of a guilty man. The return to the Father overturns that verdict (John 16:10).
Judgment, because the prince of this world has been judged. Past tense, before the cross even happens. The serpent's head was promised to be crushed from the beginning (John 16:11, Genesis 3:15).
"I have yet many things to tell you, but you can't bear them now." He paces what He tells them. Some truth has to wait until a person can carry it (John 16:12).
"He will guide you into all truth." A guide walks with you on a road. The psalmist prayed for the same thing: guide me in your truth, and teach me (John 16:13, Psalm 25:5).
"He will not speak from himself." The Spirit points away from Himself to the Son, as the Son points to the Father. Nobody in this Gospel speaks on his own authority (John 16:13-14, 7:16).
"A little while" is said seven times in four verses. The disciples keep repeating it to each other because they cannot make sense of it. Three days is a little while (John 16:16-19).

"You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice." That is the weekend of the cross exactly - and the next line is your sorrow will be turned into joy, not replaced by it. The same thing that caused the grief becomes the joy (John 16:20).
The woman in labor is a picture the prophets used for the birth of something new out of pain. Isaiah sets it right before your dead shall live (John 16:21, Isaiah 26:17-19).
"No one will take your joy away from you." Joy that comes from a resurrection cannot be undone by anything less (John 16:22).
"Whatever you may ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you." In my name is the new thing. They had prayed before; they had never prayed like this (John 16:23-24).
"The Father himself loves you." He does not have to persuade a reluctant Father on their behalf. The Father already loves them (John 16:26-27).
"I came out from the Father, and have come into the world. Again, I leave the world, and go to the Father." The whole Gospel in two sentences (John 16:28).
"Now you speak plainly." They think they finally understand. Within hours they will scatter (John 16:29-32).
"You will be scattered, everyone to his own place, and you will leave me alone." Zechariah said it: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (John 16:32, Zechariah 13:7).

"Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me." Said before the hours on the cross when He will cry out from the psalm about being forsaken - which the other Gospels record and John does not (John 16:32, Mark 15:34).
"In the world you have oppression." The word means pressure, crushing, the squeezing of grapes. He does not promise it away (John 16:33).
"Cheer up! I have overcome the world." Said by a man about to be arrested, tried, beaten and crucified - in the past tense (John 16:33).

intro: The last words before the garden prepare the disciples for what is coming. They will be put out of the synagogues, and men will kill them believing they serve God, as Saul of Tarsus later confessed he had done. Earlier that night Peter asked where He was going; now grief has so filled them that no one asks. So He offers the strangest comfort in the Gospel: it is to their advantage that He go, because otherwise the Counselor will not come. Bound to a body He was in one place at a time; the Spirit will be with all of them everywhere.

The Spirit will convict the world of sin, because they do not believe in Him; of righteousness, because He goes to the Father, overturning the verdict of the cross; and of judgment, because the prince of this world has been judged - in the past tense, before the cross has happened. He has more to tell them than they can bear, and the Spirit will guide them into all truth, speaking not on His own authority but glorifying the Son.

A little while, and they will not see Him; a little while, and they will. They repeat the phrase to one another, baffled, seven times in four verses; it is three days. They will weep while the world rejoices, and their sorrow will be turned into joy - not replaced but transformed, the cause of grief becoming the cause of joy. Like a woman in labor who forgets the anguish when the child is born, and like Isaiah's travailing people whose pangs give way to your dead shall live, their joy will be something no one can take from them.

They are to ask the Father in His name, and He tells them He need not plead with the Father for them, since the Father Himself loves them. He came from the Father and returns to Him. When they claim at last to understand, He tells them they will be scattered and leave Him alone, as Zechariah said of the struck shepherd - yet He will not be alone, for the Father is with Him. In the world they will have pressure; in Him, peace. And He tells them to take courage, because He has overcome the world, speaking in the past tense on the night of His arrest.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 17 - The Prayer Before the Garden, the Glory Before the World, and That They May Be One
chapters.title: The Prayer Before the Garden, the Glory Before the World, and That They May Be One
keyNotes: He lifted up His eyes to heaven. The disciples are not told to close theirs. They are meant to hear every word of this prayer, and so are we (John 17:1, Psalm 123:1).

This chapter is often called the high priestly prayer. The high priest carried the names of the tribes of Israel on his shoulders and over his heart when he went in before Yahweh. Here the names are carried in prayer (John 17:9, Exodus 28:12, 28:29).
"Father, the time has come." The hour that was not yet at Cana, and arrived when the Greeks came, is now (John 17:1, 2:4, 12:23).

"This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent." Eternal life is defined here not as duration but as knowing. Jeremiah said: let him who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows me (John 17:3, Jeremiah 9:24).

Knowing, in Hebrew thought, is not information. It is the word used for the closest of all relationships. Hosea says Yahweh desires the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings (John 17:3, Hosea 6:6).

"I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do." Said before the cross, as though it were already done. Tomorrow He will say it is finished (John 17:4, 19:30).

"Glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world existed." Yahweh said in Isaiah: my glory I will not give to another. Either the Son is claiming what no creature can have, or He is not another (John 17:5, Isaiah 42:8).

"I revealed your name to the people whom you have given me." The psalm says I will declare your name to my brothers, and Hebrews puts those words in His mouth. Making the Name known was His work (John 17:6, Psalm 22:22).
"They were yours, and you have given them to me." The disciples were the Father's before they were the Son's, a gift passed from one to the other (John 17:6).
"I pray not for the world, but for those whom you have given me." Not that He does not care for the world - He came for it - but this prayer is for His own (John 17:9, 3:16).
"Keep them through your name which you have given me." The Father's name was given to the Son. Yahweh said of the angel who went before Israel: my name is in him (John 17:11, Exodus 23:21).
"That they may be one, even as we are." The unity He asks for is modeled on the unity of the Father and the Son. Not uniformity - oneness (John 17:11, 10:30).

"None of them is lost, except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled." Peter later quotes the psalms about Judas: let another take his office (John 17:12, Psalm 109:8, Acts 1:20).
"That they may have my joy made full in themselves." Joy again, on the night before the cross (John 17:13, 15:11).
"I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one." Not removal, but protection in the middle of it (John 17:15, Psalm 121:7).

"Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth." The psalm says your law is truth, and all your words are truth. To be sanctified is to be set apart, and the word does the setting apart (John 17:17, Psalm 119:142, 119:160).
"For their sakes I sanctify myself." Priests were consecrated before they could serve. He sets Himself apart for the offering He is about to make (John 17:19, Exodus 29:1).
"Not for these only, but for those also who will believe in me through their word." That is everyone who has believed since. You were prayed for, on purpose, the night before the cross (John 17:20).

"That they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you." The unity of believers is meant to be the evidence that the Father sent the Son. The world is supposed to see it (John 17:21, 17:23).
Ezekiel's two sticks, Judah and Joseph, were joined into one stick in Yahweh's hand. The prayer for oneness lands on a very old promise (John 17:21, Ezekiel 37:17).
"You loved them, even as you loved me." The Father loves those who belong to the Son with the same love He has for the Son (John 17:23).
"I desire that they also may be with me where I am, that they may see my glory." The psalmist said: I will be satisfied, when I awake, with seeing your form (John 17:24, Psalm 17:15).
"Before the foundation of the world" - the love between the Father and the Son was before there was a world to love (John 17:24).
"I made known to them your name, and will make it known." The prayer ends where it began: the Name, and the love, and Him in them (John 17:26).

intro: The chapter is a single prayer, spoken aloud with eyes lifted to heaven so that the disciples may hear it. It is often called the high priestly prayer, and the title fits: the high priest bore the names of the tribes on stones at his shoulders and over his heart whenever he went in before Yahweh, and here the Son carries His own into the Father's presence.

The hour has come, and He asks to be glorified so that He may glorify the Father. Eternal life is defined not by its length but as knowing the only true God and the one He sent - knowing in the Hebrew sense of the closest relationship, the knowledge Jeremiah calls the only true boast and Hosea prizes above burnt offerings. He has finished the work He was given, He says, the day before He cries that it is finished, and He asks for the glory He had with the Father before the world existed. Isaiah records Yahweh saying He will give His glory to no other; either the Son asks for what no creature may have, or He is not other.

He prays for the disciples whom the Father gave Him, describing as keepers of the Father's word the very men who are about to scatter. He asks that they be kept through the name the Father has given Him - as Yahweh once said of His messenger, my name is in him - and made one as the Father and Son are one. Only the son of destruction was lost, in fulfillment of Scripture. He asks not that they be taken out of the world but kept from the evil one, and sanctified in the truth, which is the Father's word; and He sanctifies Himself for their sake, as a priest set apart for his offering.

Then the prayer widens to everyone who will believe through their word - every believer since, prayed for on the night before the cross. He asks that they all be one, as the Father is in Him and He in the Father, so that the world may believe the Father sent Him; the old promise of Ezekiel's two sticks joined into one stands behind it. He asks that they be with Him where He is, to see the glory given Him in the love that was before the foundation of the world, and He ends where He began, with the Name made known and the love of the Father in them.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 18 - Across the Kidron, I Am and They Fell Back, and What Is Truth?
chapters.title: Across the Kidron, I Am and They Fell Back, and What Is Truth?
keyNotes: He crossed the brook Kidron, the valley between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. King David crossed the same brook weeping, fleeing the city after his trusted counselor Ahithophel joined the rebellion against him. Ahithophel later went home and hanged himself (John 18:1, 2 Samuel 15:23, 15:31, 17:23).
Only John calls it a garden. The first Adam fell in a garden. The last Adam was arrested in one, and will be buried in one (John 18:1, 19:41).
Judas knew the place because Yahshua often met there with His disciples. Betrayal uses what friendship knows (John 18:2).
The detachment was a Roman cohort, or part of one, with officers from the chief priests. Rome and the temple came for Him together (John 18:3, 18:12).
They came with lanterns and torches to find the light of the world (John 18:3, 8:12).
"Jesus therefore, knowing all the things that were happening to him, went out." He was not found. He stepped forward (John 18:4).

"I am he" is ego eimi once more, and this time a company of soldiers goes backward and falls to the ground at the words. The psalmist said: when evildoers came at me, they stumbled and fell (John 18:5-6, Psalm 27:2).
John notes that Judas was standing with them. He was on the wrong side of the line when the words were spoken (John 18:5).
"If therefore you seek me, let these go." John says this fulfilled His own word: of those you gave me, I have lost none. The shepherd stands between the wolf and the sheep (John 18:8-9, 17:12).
Only John names Peter as the one with the sword and Malchus as the servant who lost his ear. By the time John wrote, perhaps it no longer endangered anyone to say so (John 18:10).
"The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?" The prophets speak of the cup of Yahweh's wrath. He drinks it willingly (John 18:11, Isaiah 51:17, Psalm 75:8).

He was taken first to Annas, father-in-law of Caiaphas. Annas had been high priest years before and had been removed by the Romans, but five of his sons and his son-in-law held the office after him. He was still the power behind it (John 18:13, Luke 3:2).
Another disciple, known to the high priest, got Peter into the courtyard. Most take him to be the beloved disciple, John himself (John 18:15-16).
"Are you also one of this man's disciples?" "I am not." In the garden Yahshua said I am, and an armed company fell down. In the courtyard Peter says I am not to a servant girl (John 18:17).

The fire was a fire of coals - a charcoal fire. The word appears in only one other place in the New Testament: the charcoal fire on the beach where Yahshua restores Peter. Denied by one, restored by the other (John 18:18, 21:9).
"I spoke openly to the world... in secret I said nothing." Yahweh says the same in Isaiah: I have not spoken in secret, in a place of the land of darkness (John 18:20, Isaiah 45:19).

An officer struck Him with his hand. Micah said: they will strike the judge of Israel with a rod on the cheek. Isaiah's servant said: I gave my cheeks to those who plucked out the hair (John 18:22, Micah 5:1, Isaiah 50:6).
"If I have spoken evil, testify of the evil." He does not turn the other cheek by staying silent. He asks for a lawful charge. Meekness is not the same as having no voice (John 18:23).
The third denial comes from a relative of Malchus, the man whose ear Peter cut off. Didn't I see you in the garden with him? Then the rooster crowed (John 18:26-27).

"They themselves didn't enter into the Praetorium, that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover." On the morning of the trial the Passover had not yet been eaten. John has been consistent about this since chapter 13 (John 18:28, 13:1, 19:14).
Careful not to be defiled by a Gentile's house, they were in the middle of handing an innocent man over to be killed. The irony needs no comment (John 18:28).

"It is illegal for us to put anyone to death." Rome kept the power of execution. That is why He would die by crucifixion rather than stoning - lifted up, as He had said, the kind of death He would die (John 18:31-32, 12:32-33).

Psalm 22 describes the sufferer's hands and feet pierced - the reading of the Septuagint and of the WEB, which the Masoretic text has as like a lion. Zechariah says they will look on me whom they have pierced (John 18:32, Psalm 22:16, Zechariah 12:10).
"Are you the King of the Jews?" is Pilate's first question in all four Gospels. It was the charge Rome cared about (John 18:33).

"My Kingdom is not of this world." Not from this world - its source is elsewhere. It is not that the kingdom has nothing to do with the earth; Daniel saw it filling the earth. It does not come by the means this world uses (John 18:36, Daniel 2:44).
"If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight." One of them had already drawn a sword, and been told to put it away (John 18:36, 18:11).

"For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth." Born, and came into the world - two statements, one about birth and one about coming from somewhere else (John 18:37).
"What is truth?" Pilate asked it standing in front of the one who had said I am the truth, and walked out without waiting for an answer (John 18:38, 14:6).

"I find no basis for a charge against him." The first of three times Pilate says it. The Passover lamb had to be without defect, and the Roman judge examines Him and finds none (John 18:38, 19:4, 19:6, Exodus 12:5).

Barabbas was a robber - the word was used for bandits and violent rebels. His name means son of the father. On the Day of Atonement one goat died and the other was sent away alive. Many have seen the picture here; John simply tells what happened (John 18:40, Leviticus 16:8-10).

intro: When the prayer ends, Yahshua crosses the brook Kidron with His disciples - the brook King David crossed weeping as he fled Jerusalem, betrayed by his trusted counselor Ahithophel, who later hanged himself. The parallel needs no comment. Only John calls the place a garden: the first Adam fell in a garden, the last is arrested in one and will be buried in one. Judas knows it because Yahshua often met there with His disciples, and he comes with Roman soldiers and temple officers, carrying lanterns and torches to find the light of the world.

Knowing all that is coming, Yahshua goes out to meet them and asks whom they seek. At His answer, ego eimi, the armed company goes backward and falls to the ground - and then He lets them rise and take Him, asking only that His disciples be let go, so that He loses none of those given Him. Peter strikes off Malchus's ear and is told to sheathe the sword: the cup the Father has given must be drunk. He is bound and taken first to Annas, the deposed high priest who still held the power behind the office through his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas.

In the courtyard Peter, asked by a servant girl whether he is a disciple, says I am not - the reverse of the I am that felled the soldiers - and warms himself at a charcoal fire, a word that appears again only at the beach where he will be restored. Before Annas, Yahshua says He has spoken openly and nothing in secret, and when an officer strikes Him, as Micah foresaw the judge of Israel struck on the cheek, He asks for a lawful charge; meekness is not silence. Peter denies Him twice more, the last time to a relative of Malchus, and the rooster crows.

At dawn He is brought to the Praetorium, and His accusers will not enter lest they be defiled and unable to eat the Passover - which, as John has said since chapter 13, had not yet been eaten. Rome holds the power of death, so He will be lifted up rather than stoned, as He had said. To Pilate He says His kingdom is not from this world and does not advance by the sword, and that He was born to testify to the truth. Pilate asks what truth is, standing before the one who said He is the truth, and walks out without waiting for an answer. Three times he will find no fault in Him, as the Passover lamb had to be found without defect. The crowd asks instead for Barabbas, a violent robber whose name means son of the father.

verses.1: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered.
verses.2: Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.
verses.3: Judas then, having taken a detachment of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons.
verses.4: Jesus therefore, knowing all the things that were happening to him, went out, and said to them, “Who are you looking for?”
verses.5: They answered him, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus said to them, “I am he.” Judas also, who betrayed him, was standing with them.
verses.6: When therefore he said to them, “I am he,” they went backward, and fell to the ground.
verses.7: Again therefore he asked them, “Who are you looking for?” They said, “Jesus of Nazareth.”
verses.8: Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. If therefore you seek me, let these go their way,”
verses.9: that the word might be fulfilled which he spoke, “Of those whom you have given me, I have lost none.”
verses.10: Simon Peter therefore, having a sword, drew it, and struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.
verses.11: Jesus therefore said to Peter, “Put the sword into its sheath. The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?”
verses.12: So the detachment, the commanding officer, and the officers of the Jews, seized Jesus and bound him,
verses.13: and led him to Annas first, for he was father-in-law to Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.
verses.14: Now it was Caiaphas who advised the Jews that it was expedient that one man should perish for the people.
verses.15: Simon Peter followed Jesus, as did another disciple. Now that disciple was known to the high priest, and entered in with Jesus into the court of the high priest;
verses.16: but Peter was standing at the door outside. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to her who kept the door, and brought in Peter.
verses.17: Then the maid who kept the door said to Peter, “Are you also one of this man’s disciples?” He said, “I am not.”
verses.18: Now the servants and the officers were standing there, having made a fire of coals, for it was cold. They were warming themselves. Peter was with them, standing and warming himself.
verses.19: The high priest therefore asked Jesus about his disciples, and about his teaching.
verses.20: Jesus answered him, “I spoke openly to the world. I always taught in synagogues, and in the temple, where the Jews always meet. I said nothing in secret.
verses.21: Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them. Behold, these know the things which I said.”
verses.22: When he had said this, one of the officers standing by slapped Jesus with his hand, saying, “Do you answer the high priest like that?”
verses.23: Jesus answered him, “If I have spoken evil, testify of the evil; but if well, why do you beat me?”
verses.24: Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas, the high priest.
verses.25: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. They said therefore to him, “You aren’t also one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it, and said, “I am not.”
verses.26: One of the servants of the high priest, being a relative of him whose ear Peter had cut off, said, “Didn’t I see you in the garden with him?”
verses.27: Peter therefore denied it again, and immediately the rooster crowed.
verses.28: They led Jesus therefore from Caiaphas into the Praetorium. It was early, and they themselves didn’t enter into the Praetorium, that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.
verses.29: Pilate therefore went out to them, and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”
verses.30: They answered him, “If this man weren’t an evildoer, we wouldn’t have delivered him up to you.”
verses.31: Pilate therefore said to them, “Take him yourselves, and judge him according to your law.” Therefore the Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death,”
verses.32: that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what kind of death he should die.
verses.33: Pilate therefore entered again into the Praetorium, called Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”
verses.34: Jesus answered him, “Do you say this by yourself, or did others tell you about me?”
verses.35: Pilate answered, “I’m not a Jew, am I? Your own nation and the chief priests delivered you to me. What have you done?”
verses.36: Jesus answered, “My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews. But now my Kingdom is not from here.”
verses.37: Pilate therefore said to him, “Are you a king then?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”
verses.38: Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” When he had said this, he went out again to the Jews, and said to them, “I find no basis for a charge against him.
verses.39: But you have a custom, that I should release someone to you at the Passover. Therefore, do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”
verses.40: Then they all shouted again, saying, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.

chapters.title: Behold the Man, It Is Finished, and a Tomb in a Garden
keyNotes: Pilate had Him flogged before any verdict, probably hoping a beating would satisfy the crowd. It did not (John 19:1, 19:4-6).
The crown was woven from thorns. Thorns came into the world with the curse on the ground in Genesis 3. The one who came to undo the curse wore it on His head (John 19:2, Genesis 3:17-18).

"Behold, the man!" Pilate means look at him - beaten, harmless, pitiful. Zechariah had said: behold, the man whose name is the Branch, and he shall build Yahweh's temple. Pilate quoted a prophet without knowing it (John 19:5, Zechariah 6:12).
"I find no basis for a charge against him" is said for the second and third times here. The Lamb examined by the judge three times, and found without defect (John 19:4, 19:6, 18:38).
"By our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God." Now the real charge comes out. Not sedition. Blasphemy (John 19:7, Leviticus 24:16).

When he heard that, Pilate was more afraid. Romans had stories about sons of gods walking among men. Where are you from? - and Yahshua gives him no answer, as the servant before his shearers was silent (John 19:8-9, Isaiah 53:7).
"You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above." The governor thinks he holds the power. He is told where it comes from (John 19:11).
"You aren't Caesar's friend." Friend of Caesar was an honored title, and a threat: a governor reported to Rome for freeing a would-be king would lose everything (John 19:12).
The judgment seat stood on a stone pavement called Gabbatha. John gives both the Greek and the Hebrew name, as an eyewitness would (John 19:13).

"It was the Preparation Day of the Passover" - the day the lambs were made ready. Mark places the crucifixion at the third hour and John has Pilate's verdict at about the sixth; whether John counts hours differently or both are approximate, readers have long discussed (John 19:14, Mark 15:25).

"Behold, your King!" And the chief priests answer: we have no king but Caesar. The men who led the worship of Yahweh rejected Him as King out loud, as Israel did when they asked Samuel for a king like the nations (John 19:14-15, 1 Samuel 8:7).
"He went out, bearing his cross." Isaac carried the wood up Moriah on his own back. John does not mention Simon of Cyrene; he wants you to see the Son carrying the wood (John 19:17, Genesis 22:6).
Golgotha means the place of a skull. It was outside the city, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp (John 19:17, 19:20, Hebrews 13:11-12).
Two others were crucified with Him, one on each side, and Yahshua in the middle. Numbered with the transgressors, as Isaiah said (John 19:18, Isaiah 53:12).

The sign read JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS in Hebrew, Latin and Greek - the language of the covenant, of the empire, and of the wider world. Everybody passing by could read it (John 19:19-20).
"What I have written, I have written." Pilate, who could not stand up for the truth, would not change a sign that told it (John 19:22).

The soldiers split His clothes four ways, and gambled for the seamless tunic, woven from the top in one piece. The robe of the high priest was woven work, made so it would not be torn. The psalm says: they divide my garments among them, and cast lots for my clothing (John 19:23-24, Exodus 28:32, Psalm 22:18).
Women stood by the cross, and one disciple. Most of the men who had promised to die with Him were gone (John 19:25-26).
"Woman, behold your son!" The same address He used at Cana. His mother appears at the first sign and at the cross, and at both He calls her woman (John 19:26, 2:4).
From the cross He provides for His mother. Honor your father and your mother - kept to His last breath (John 19:26-27, Exodus 20:12).

"I am thirsty." The one who offered living water at a well and shouted come and drink at the feast, thirsty. In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink, the psalm says (John 19:28, 4:14, 7:37, Psalm 69:21).
The sponge was put on hyssop - the plant used to paint the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts in Egypt. John alone mentions it (John 19:29, Exodus 12:22).
"It is finished" is one word in Greek, tetelestai, which could be written on a bill to mean paid in full. It is from the same root as loved them to the end in 13:1 (John 19:30, 13:1).
"He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit." He was not overcome. He handed His spirit over. No one took His life from Him (John 19:30, 10:18).

"That Sabbath was a special one" - in older translations, a high day. That is the language of an annual Sabbath, and the first day of Unleavened Bread was a holy convocation with no regular work. This study reads it that way, which places two Sabbaths in that week and leaves room for three days and three nights in the tomb (John 19:31, Leviticus 23:6-7, Matthew 12:40).
Bodies were not to hang overnight, because the Torah says a hanged man must be buried the same day. Breaking the legs made death come quickly (John 19:31, Deuteronomy 21:22-23).
They did not break His legs, because He was already dead. A bone of the Passover lamb was not to be broken (John 19:33, 19:36, Exodus 12:46, Psalm 34:20).
A soldier pierced His side, and blood and water came out. John stops the story to swear that he saw it - he who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true (John 19:34-35).
"They will look on him whom they pierced" is Zechariah 12, where Yahweh is speaking: they will look to me whom they have pierced. John quotes it of the man on the cross (John 19:37, Zechariah 12:10).
Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple for fear of the Jews, asks for the body. Nicodemus, who first came by night, comes with him. The cross brought the hidden ones into the open (John 19:38-39).

A hundred Roman pounds of myrrh and aloes is about seventy-five pounds by our measure - a burial fit for a king. The psalm says all your garments smell of myrrh and aloes (John 19:39, Psalm 45:8, 2 Chronicles 16:14).
The tomb was new, in a garden, and no one had ever been laid in it. Isaiah said His grave would be with a rich man in His death (John 19:41, Isaiah 53:9, Matthew 27:57).

intro: Pilate has Yahshua flogged, and the soldiers crown Him with thorns - the mark of the curse laid on the ground in Genesis 3, now worn by the one who came to undo it - and mock Him in purple. Pilate leads Him out with the words behold, the man, meaning only that so pitiful a figure could be no threat, and repeating unawares Zechariah's announcement of the man whose name is the Branch, who would build the temple of Yahweh. Twice more Pilate declares he finds no fault in Him. The Lamb is examined three times and found without defect.

Then the true charge emerges: He made Himself the Son of God. Pilate, frightened, asks where He is from and receives no answer, the silence of the servant before his shearers. Told that his power comes from above, and threatened with the loss of Caesar's friendship, Pilate sits in judgment on the Preparation Day of the Passover, as the lambs were being made ready, and presents Him as their King. The chief priests answer that they have no king but Caesar - the rejection of Yahweh's kingship that Samuel heard when Israel asked for a king like the nations.

He goes out carrying His own cross, as Isaac carried the wood up Moriah, and is crucified between two others, numbered with the transgressors. Pilate's sign names Him King of the Jews in Hebrew, Latin and Greek, and he will not alter it. The soldiers divide His garments and cast lots for the seamless tunic, as Psalm 22 foretold. From the cross He gives His mother into the care of the disciple He loved, keeping the commandment to honor her to His last breath. He thirsts - He who offered living water - and is given vinegar on hyssop, the plant that marked the Passover blood on the doorposts. Then He says tetelestai, it is finished, paid in full, and gives up His spirit.

The day was the Preparation, and the coming Sabbath a special one, the language of an annual Sabbath; this study reads it as the first day of Unleavened Bread, which makes two Sabbaths that week and room for three days and three nights in the tomb. The legs of the others are broken, but not His, for He is already dead and no bone of the Passover lamb was to be broken. A spear pierces His side, blood and water flow, and John swears to what he saw, citing Zechariah's they will look on him whom they pierced - spoken there by Yahweh of Himself. Then Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, disciples who had hidden, come into the open and bury Him with a king's weight of spices in a new tomb in a garden.

verses.1: So Pilate then took Jesus, and flogged him.
verses.2: The soldiers twisted thorns into a crown, and put it on his head, and dressed him in a purple garment.
verses.3: They kept saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and they kept slapping him.
verses.4: Then Pilate went out again, and said to them, “Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no basis for a charge against him.”
verses.5: Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. Pilate said to them, “Behold, the man!”
verses.6: When therefore the chief priests and the officers saw him, they shouted, saying, “Crucify! Crucify!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves, and crucify him, for I find no basis for a charge against him.”
verses.7: The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”
verses.8: When therefore Pilate heard this saying, he was more afraid.
verses.9: He entered into the Praetorium again, and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.
verses.10: Pilate therefore said to him, “Aren’t you speaking to me? Don’t you know that I have power to release you, and have power to crucify you?”
verses.11: Jesus answered, “You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above. Therefore he who delivered me to you has greater sin.”
verses.12: At this, Pilate was seeking to release him, but the Jews cried out, saying, “If you release this man, you aren’t Caesar’s friend! Everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar!”
verses.13: When Pilate therefore heard these words, he brought Jesus out, and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called “The Pavement”, but in Hebrew, “Gabbatha.”
verses.14: Now it was the Preparation Day of the Passover, at about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold, your King!”
verses.15: They cried out, “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar!”
verses.16: So then he delivered him to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus and led him away.
verses.17: He went out, bearing his cross, to the place called “The Place of a Skull”, which is called in Hebrew, “Golgotha”,
verses.18: where they crucified him, and with him two others, on either side one, and Jesus in the middle.
verses.19: Pilate wrote a title also, and put it on the cross. There was written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
verses.20: Therefore many of the Jews read this title, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek.
verses.21: The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate, “Don’t write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but, ‘he said, “I am King of the Jews.”’”
verses.22: Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”
verses.23: Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also the coat. Now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.
verses.24: Then they said to one another, “Let’s not tear it, but cast lots for it to decide whose it will be,” that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says, “They parted my garments among them. For my cloak they cast lots.” Therefore the soldiers did these things.
verses.25: But there were standing by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
verses.26: Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”
verses.27: Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.
verses.28: After this, Jesus, seeing that all things were now finished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, “I am thirsty.”
verses.29: Now a vessel full of vinegar was set there; so they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop, and held it at his mouth.
verses.30: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.
verses.31: Therefore the Jews, because it was the Preparation Day, so that the bodies wouldn’t remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a special one), asked of Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away.
verses.32: Therefore the soldiers came, and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who was crucified with him;
verses.33: but when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they didn’t break his legs.
verses.34: However one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.
verses.35: He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe.
verses.36: For these things happened, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, “A bone of him will not be broken.”
verses.37: Again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they pierced.”
verses.38: After these things, Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked of Pilate that he might take away Jesus’ body. Pilate gave him permission. He came therefore and took away his body.
verses.39: Nicodemus, who at first came to Jesus by night, also came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds.
verses.40: So they took Jesus’ body, and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury.
verses.41: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. In the garden was a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid.
verses.42: Then because of the Jews’ Preparation Day (for the tomb was near at hand) they laid Jesus there.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 20 - An Empty Tomb Before Dawn, Mary in the Garden, and My Lord and My God
chapters.title: An Empty Tomb Before Dawn, Mary in the Garden, and My Lord and My God
keyNotes: "On the first day of the week... while it was still dark." Mary came early and the stone was already gone. Nobody in any Gospel sees the resurrection happen. They find it already done (John 20:1).

The first day of the week, after the Sabbath, was the day the firstfruits sheaf was waved before Yahweh during Unleavened Bread. Paul calls the risen Messiah the firstfruits of those who are asleep (John 20:1, Leviticus 23:10-11, 1 Corinthians 15:20).

"They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb." Her first thought is grave robbery. Nobody expected a resurrection, which is one reason the accounts read as reports rather than inventions (John 20:2).
The other disciple outran Peter and got there first. John tells on himself - he got there first and waited outside; Peter, being Peter, went straight in (John 20:4-6).

The linen cloths were lying there, and the cloth that had been on His head was rolled up in a place by itself. Thieves do not unwrap a body and fold the cloth. Lazarus came out still wrapped. Yahshua left the wrappings behind (John 20:5-7, 11:44).
"He saw and believed." Before any appearance, before any angel spoke to him, the beloved disciple believed from what was left in the tomb (John 20:8).

"They still didn't know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead." The Scriptures had said it - you will not let your holy one see corruption, on the third day he will raise us up - and they had not put it together (John 20:9, Psalm 16:10, Hosea 6:2).
Mary stays when the men go home. She is weeping outside the tomb, and she stoops to look in (John 20:10-11).

Two angels in white, one at the head and one at the feet of where the body had lain. Over the ark of the covenant, two cherubim faced each other from either end of the mercy seat, and Yahweh said: there I will meet with you (John 20:12, Exodus 25:18-22).
"Woman, why are you weeping?" asked by the angels and then by Yahshua. Her grief is taken seriously, and questioned (John 20:13, 20:15).

She supposed Him to be the gardener. It is a garden, and in a sense she was right. The first man was put in a garden to tend it. The last Adam walks in one on the morning of the new creation (John 20:15, Genesis 2:15).
"Mary." One word. The good shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and they know his voice (John 20:16, 10:3).
"Rabboni" means my teacher, a warmer form than Rabbi. John translates it, as he translated Rabbi and Messiah in chapter 1 (John 20:16, 1:38).
"Don't hold me" can mean stop clinging to me. She has Him back and does not want to let go. He has somewhere to go and something for her to do (John 20:17).

"I haven't yet ascended to my Father." Many connect this with the firstfruits sheaf, which had to be presented before Yahweh to be accepted. The text says only that He had not yet ascended (John 20:17, Leviticus 23:11).
"Go to my brothers." For the first time in this Gospel He calls the disciples brothers. My Father and your Father, my God and your God. The cross made them family (John 20:17, Psalm 22:22).
Mary Magdalene is the first person in the Gospel to see the risen Lord and the first sent to tell about it. I have seen the Lord (John 20:18).
That evening the doors were locked for fear. He came and stood in the middle. Locked doors did not keep Him out, and fear did not keep Him away (John 20:19).
"Peace be to you" was the ordinary greeting, shalom. On that night, from Him, to the men who ran, it was not ordinary at all. He said it twice (John 20:19, 20:21).
He showed them His hands and His side. The risen body still carries the wounds. Isaiah said: I have engraved you on the palms of my hands (John 20:20, Isaiah 49:16).
"As the Father has sent me, even so I send you." Their mission is modeled on His (John 20:21, 17:18).

"He breathed on them." The word is the one used when Yahweh God breathed into the man's nostrils the breath of life, and Ezekiel prophesied to the breath to breathe on the slain so they would live. New creation, in a locked room (John 20:22, Genesis 2:7, Ezekiel 37:9).
"If you forgive anyone's sins, they have been forgiven them." The first thing the risen Lord hands His people is the work of forgiveness. It is where deliverance starts (John 20:23).
Thomas was not there. Unless I see the print of the nails, and put my hand into His side, I will not believe. He asked for what the others had already been given (John 20:24-25).
"After eight days" - by their counting, the next first day of the week. He comes again to the same room and goes straight to Thomas (John 20:26).
He offers Thomas exactly what Thomas demanded, word for word. He had heard every word of the doubt without being in the room (John 20:27, 20:25).

"My Lord and my God!" is the highest confession in the Gospels, and it comes from the doubter. The psalmist prayed rise up to defend me, my God, my Lord. Yahshua does not correct him (John 20:28, Psalm 35:23).
The Gospel began with the Word was God and nearly ends with a man calling Him my God. John 1:1 and John 20:28 are the frame of the book (John 20:28, 1:1).
"Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed." That is everyone who has believed since - including everyone reading this (John 20:29).

"These are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name." John tells you why he wrote the book. Everything he chose was chosen for this (John 20:30-31).

intro: On the first day of the week, while it is still dark, Mary Magdalene finds the stone already removed. No one in any Gospel witnesses the resurrection itself; it is found already accomplished. The day is the one after the Sabbath on which, during Unleavened Bread, the firstfruits sheaf was waved before Yahweh, and Paul would call the risen Messiah the firstfruits of those who sleep. Mary assumes robbery and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, who race to the tomb. John records that he arrived first and waited, and that Peter went straight in. The linen lies in place and the head cloth is rolled up apart - no thief's work, and a contrast with Lazarus, who came out bound. The beloved disciple sees and believes, though none of them yet understood the Scriptures that He must rise.

Mary remains, weeping, and sees two angels where the body had lain, one at the head and one at the feet, like the cherubim at either end of the mercy seat where Yahweh promised to meet with Israel. She mistakes the risen Lord for the gardener - not wholly wrongly, in a garden on the first morning of the new creation - until He speaks her name, as the shepherd calls his own sheep. She clings to Him and is told to let go: He has not yet ascended, and she is to tell His brothers - the first time He calls them that - that He ascends to His Father and theirs, His God and theirs. She becomes the first to announce that she has seen the Lord.

That evening He stands among the disciples behind locked doors and gives them peace, twice, showing the wounds in His hands and side. As the Father sent Him, He sends them, and He breathes on them - the verb of Yahweh breathing life into Adam and of Ezekiel's breath upon the slain - saying receive the Holy Spirit, and entrusting them with the forgiveness of sins, which is where deliverance begins.

Thomas, absent, demands to touch the wounds. Eight days later Yahshua returns and offers him the exact terms of his doubt, which He had heard without being present. Thomas answers my Lord and my God, and is not corrected; the Gospel that opened with the Word was God closes its account with a man calling Him my God. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe - every reader since. And John states his purpose: these things are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and believing have life in His name.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 21 - A Night of Catching Nothing, Breakfast on the Beach, and Do You Love Me?
chapters.title: A Night of Catching Nothing, Breakfast on the Beach, and Do You Love Me?
keyNotes: Chapter 20 ended with a purpose statement that sounds like a conclusion. Chapter 21 reads like an epilogue, added to tell what happened to Peter and to correct a rumor about the beloved disciple (John 21:1, 20:31, 21:23).
Seven disciples are there, and Nathanael of Cana is named - the man from chapter 1, who has not been mentioned since (John 21:2, 1:45-49).
"I'm going fishing." Peter goes back to what he knew before he was called. The others go with him. That night they caught nothing (John 21:3).

It is the same scene as the day He first called Peter in Luke: a night of nothing, a word to let the nets down, and more fish than the net could hold. He is calling Peter again, the same way (John 21:3-6, Luke 5:5-6).
"Children, have you anything to eat?" He calls them children, little ones, the way a father would. They answer with one word: no (John 21:5).
"Cast the net on the right side of the boat." A hundred yards from shore, on the side they had presumably already tried. The difference was not the location. It was the word (John 21:6).
"It's the Lord!" The beloved disciple recognizes Him first; Peter acts first. He throws on his coat and jumps into the water. The two of them, true to form (John 21:7).

A fire of coals, with fish and bread already on it. The charcoal fire is the same word as the fire in the high priest's courtyard where Peter denied Him. The only two in the New Testament (John 21:9, 18:18).
Fish and bread, the same food as the feeding of the five thousand. He takes the bread and gives it to them, and the fish likewise (John 21:9, 21:13, 6:11).
"Bring some of the fish which you have just caught." He already has fish on the fire. He asks for theirs anyway. He wants their part in it (John 21:10).

A hundred and fifty-three large fish, counted. It is the kind of thing a fisherman remembers. Many symbolic readings have been offered; the text offers none. And the net was not torn, though in the earlier catch the nets were breaking (John 21:11, Luke 5:6).
Ezekiel saw a river flowing from the temple, and fishermen spreading their nets, and fish exceedingly many. The catch is a picture of what the mission will bring in (John 21:11, Ezekiel 47:9-10).
"Come and eat breakfast." The risen Lord of all creation cooks breakfast for men who abandoned Him (John 21:12).
"None of the disciples dared inquire of him, 'Who are you?' knowing that it was the Lord." He is the same and not the same, recognized and yet changed (John 21:12).
"Simon, son of Jonah" - not Peter, the rock. The name he had before he was called. Three times (John 21:15-17, 1:42).

"Do you love me more than these?" More than these men, or more than these fish and boats? Peter had once claimed more than the others: even if all fall away, I will not. Now he does not compare himself to anyone (John 21:15, Mark 14:29).

The WEB shows a change in the Greek. Twice Yahshua asks do you love me, using agapao, and Peter answers I have affection for you, using phileo. The third time Yahshua takes Peter's own word. Readers debate how much weight to give it, since John uses both words for the Father's love for the Son (John 21:15-17, 3:35, 5:20).
Three questions for three denials. He does not skip the wound, and He does not leave it open (John 21:17, 18:17, 18:25, 18:27).
"Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time." Restoration can hurt. The grief is part of the healing (John 21:17).
"Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you." Peter no longer trusts his own promises. He appeals to what the Lord knows (John 21:17).
Feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep. The man who failed is given the flock. Restoration in this Gospel is not probation; it is a commission (John 21:15-17, 10:11).

"When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you." John explains it meant the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. Early tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome. Peter himself later wrote that the putting off of his tent was near, as the Lord had shown him (John 21:18-19, 2 Peter 1:14).
"Follow me." The first words He spoke to His first followers in chapter 1 were come and see; the last words He says to Peter are follow me (John 21:19, 1:39).
"Lord, what about this man?" Peter, just restored, immediately looks at somebody else's path. "What is that to you? You follow me" (John 21:21-22).

A rumor spread that the beloved disciple would not die. John corrects it carefully: Yahshua never said that. He said if I desire that he stay until I come. Even at the end, John insists on exactly what was said (John 21:23).
"This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true." The beloved disciple is the author, and others vouch for him (John 21:24).
"Even the world itself wouldn't have room for the books." John chose a handful of signs out of a life too large to write down - and chose them so that you might believe (John 21:25, 20:30-31).

intro: The Gospel seemed to close with its purpose statement, but John adds an epilogue, because Peter's story is unfinished. Seven disciples are by the Sea of Tiberias, Nathanael of Cana among them, and Peter announces that he is going fishing - back to the life before his call, perhaps believing after the courtyard that it was all he was fit for. They fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a man on the shore, unrecognised, calls them children, asks if they have caught anything, and tells them to cast on the right side. The net fills beyond hauling - the very scene of Peter's first call in Luke, repeated to call him again.

The beloved disciple recognises Him first, and Peter, as at the tomb, acts first, plunging into the sea. On the shore is a charcoal fire, with fish and bread - the word used only here and for the fire where Peter denied Him, and the food of the five thousand. He asks for some of their catch though He has fish already cooking. The catch is counted, a hundred and fifty-three, and the net holds, as Ezekiel's fishermen spread their nets by the river from the temple among fish exceedingly many. Then the risen Lord serves breakfast to the men who had abandoned Him.

After the meal He addresses Peter by his old name, Simon son of Jonah, and asks three times whether Peter loves Him. Peter, who once claimed to love Him more than all the others, now compares himself to no one, and answers with a humbler word than the one he was asked - which the WEB preserves - until the third time Yahshua takes up Peter's own word. Three questions answer three denials, and Peter is grieved, because restoration does not skip the wound; but he appeals no longer to his own promises, only to the Lord's knowledge of him. Each answer is followed by a charge to feed or tend the flock. The man who failed is given the sheep. Restoration is a commission, not a probation.

Yahshua tells Peter that in old age he will stretch out his hands and be led where he would not go, signifying the death by which he would glorify God, and says follow Me. Peter at once asks about the beloved disciple, and is told that whatever is decided for that man, his part is to follow. John corrects the rumor that this disciple would not die, insisting on exactly what was said, and the book closes with the testimony of its author, vouched for by others, and the confession that the world itself could not contain the books if everything He did were written.
